extensionPoints.description: A tab on the signed-in person's own profile page (/me): something about the person that another module owns, such as billing details, passkeys, signing certificates or connected messaging channels. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'user.profile.tabs': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'user.profile.tabs', component, order, scope, props: { label } }. Props received: { tenantId, label }. The label is the tab title and the contribution id is the tab id; a contribution that has nothing to show for this person renders an empty state, not nothing, because the tab is already visible.

The PUSH side, out of accounting into a third-party bookkeeping system (Logo, and others as they're built) — the mirror image of accounting:posting. A contributor is a SANDBOXED community plugin, resolved via the same external-contributions bridge payment/notification_sms/calendar use for their sandboxed gateways (never an in-tree exporter). Op: exportJournalEntry({ entry: ExportJournalEntry }) => Promise<void>, invoked fire-and-forget by AccountingPostingService.post AFTER a journal entry is durably POSTED — a slow or failing exporter must never delay or fail the posting call a money module is waiting on. ExportJournalEntry carries the entry (number/date/description/currency/source) and its lines (account code/name, side, major-unit amount). Nothing retries a failed export yet; that is a tracked gap, not a promise this seam makes.

Where a money module records a double-entry journal for a document it owns (invoice issued, payment captured) WITHOUT importing accounting. Default export: (tenantId, req: PostingRequest) => Promise<PostingResult>, where req carries role-based lines (revenue/tax_payable/accounts_receivable/cash) in minor units; accounting resolves the roles to the tenant's mapped ledger accounts and writes ONE balanced, POSTED entry, idempotent on (sourceType,sourceId). Declared so accounting never imports invoice/payment/90 money modules (the arrow would be backwards) and callers stay decoupled — a caller looks the sink up via the registry. gate 'data' (EXT-1, an internal planning document): a posting is a bookkeeping duty for a document already issued, so it keeps reaching the ledger while accounting is switched off, unentitled or uninstalled, until its data is purged; a tenant that never mapped a chart of accounts gets a skip, as before. Fails SOFT: a missing mapping or an error is a skip, never a thrown error into the money flow.

A domain module's AI-drivable action on its OWN records. Default export: { actionType ('<module>.<verb>'), subjectType, label, description?, plan(tenantId, subjectId) => Promise<{summary, proposedChange, confidence} | null>, execute(tenantId, subjectId, proposedChange) => Promise<void> }. The runtime calls plan() to get a proposal and, once a human approves it (mode SUGGEST) or if the tenant chose AUTO, calls execute() — which is the CONTRIBUTOR's code writing its own records. ai_agent never writes into another module's tables, the same rule crm_assignment holds ('the decision-maker writes nothing'). plan() answering null means 'nothing to propose about this record', which is the common case and is not an error. `confidence` is recorded and shown, never gated on: a threshold is a policy decision and the question of whether an agent may write with no human at all is still open. The frozen proposal on the run row is what execute() receives, so approving a suggestion cannot become approving a re-roll.

An action the responder may take through the module that owns it (an internal planning document §1.5, 05): end a session, lock an account, ban an address, revoke a key. Default export: one FirewallActionContribution or an array ({ id '<module>.<verb>', rung, lanes, actorKinds, ttl { defaultMs, maxMs }, minimumMode suggest | auto, defaultMode?, hourlyBudget, evidence { boundToActor, minSignals, kinds? }, execute(ctx), undo(ctx) }); import the type from common/server/common.firewall-contracts. The owning module's own service does the work; ai_firewall writes no other module's table. metadata: { label, ids: the action ids it registers }. Boot refuses (the ai-firewall-registries guard) an action without undo (FWA-4), a human rung (step_up, end_session, end_all_sessions, lock) on a machine or device lane, a step-up on a lane whose LANE_POLICY has no step-up and an address actor on a lane that never bans addresses (FWA-6), a ttl.maxMs above the platform cap (30 days), end_all_sessions or lock without evidence bound to the actor (FWA-5), an evidence kind no ai_firewall:signal contribution registers, an id that names another module, and a duplicate id. Every action is Observe on install; a tenant's mode per action and the kill switches are ai_firewall's settings.

The optional language-model analyst (an internal planning document §1.5, 06): incident triage, the digest, questions over events. Default export: a FirewallAnalyst ({ key, available(tenantId), triage(incident, allowed), digest(tenantId, period, facts), toFilter(tenantId, question) }, every method may answer null); import the type from common/server/common.firewall-contracts. Contributed by the Pro module ai; a Core install has none and explains from templates. It advises only: its triage can create a Suggest item, never an automatic action (FWA-11), and its output is constrained to the registered action ids (FWA-3). Select with fallback none: at most one provider; boot refuses (the ai-firewall-registries guard) a second one, since the firewall would not know which one triages.

A decoy a module owns (an internal planning document §1.5, 02 §2.5): a key, a record, a route or a credential nobody legitimate touches. Default export: one HoneytokenContribution or an array ({ id '<module>.<decoy>', kind, labelKey, detector { signalKind }, plant?(tenantId), remove?(tenantId) }); import the type from common/server/common.firewall-contracts. The owning module emits detector.signalKind (severity critical; emitHoneytokenTouch in the contract) when the decoy is touched, and answers a touch exactly as it answers what the decoy pretends to be (a wrong key, a missing record, a missing route). plant(tenantId) answers { ref, bait?, where? } for the canary list (GET /api/ai-firewall/honeytokens, the only place a decoy is shown); no list, count or export a customer reads may show a decoy. metadata: { label, ids: the decoy ids }. Boot refuses (the ai-firewall-registries guard) a decoy without a detector, a detector whose signal kind no ai_firewall:signal contribution registers or registers below critical, an id that names another module and a duplicate id.

The signal kinds a module emits (an internal planning document §1.5): what the firewall may read, and the vocabulary of its rules, models and pages. Default export: one FirewallSignalContribution or an array ({ kind, labelKey?, lanes, actorKinds, outcomes?, severity, defaultWeight 0..1, attrs: { <name>: { type: string | number | boolean | untrusted, pd: none | identifier | network | device | location | contact | content } } }); import the type from common/server/common.firewall-contracts, never from ai_firewall. metadata: { label, ids: the kinds it registers (exactly those the export lists), routes?: the human auth routes whose outcome these kinds record (npm run check:firewall-signal-coverage), records?: kinds another contribution registers that record the outcome of those routes too (a passkey sign-in ends in user_session.login; each must be registered) }. The kinds of audit rows are the audit actions (auditRowSignal in the contract adds the row's attributes); each kind is registered by the module that owns the action. The snapshot refuses a kind two contributions list (uniqueMetadata ids); boot refuses (the ai-firewall-registries guard) a kind registered twice, ids the export and the manifest disagree on, a malformed kind and an attribute without a personal-data class. Loaded in a system context, process-wide, by the boot guard and on first use; never while a module evaluates (lazyContributors). Contributing is not depending: a Pro, Enterprise or IoT module contributes from its own folder and ai_firewall imports none of its contributors.

A backend AI provider (chat / embeddings / streaming). Providers come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @openai/gpt, @anthropic/claude in modules/marketplace/examples); no in-tree module provides one, and the host reads plugins only.

A module that wants to hear about tracked events as they land. Default export: { key?, names?: string[], onEvent(tenantId, event) } where event is { eventId, name, userId, anonymousId, sessionId, properties, path, occurredAt }. `names` narrows the subscription and a sink without it hears everything — say it out loud. Dispatched FIRE-AND-FORGET after the event row is saved: `track()` sits on the request path of every page view and click, so a sink that is slow, broken or missing must never turn that into a failed write. Each sink is isolated; a throw is logged and dropped. Direction is the usual one — analytics owns events and knows nothing about who listens, so a gamification rule engine subscribes here rather than analytics importing a badge.

An audience axis of a platform announcement that another module knows (D18): the contribution's `key` is the facet id the audience stores its values under (`plan`: tenant_subscription, the tenants whose live subscription is on a chosen plan; `edition`: module_lifecycle, the tenants using an active module of a chosen edition), `metadata.label` its name in the composer. Default export: { options() => Promise<{ value, label }[]>, tenantsMatching(values) => Promise<tenantId[]> } (AudienceFacetProvider in server/announcement.types.ts). The composer lists every facet's options; a send narrows its tenants to those that match ANY value of each facet it uses. Fails CLOSED for a facet in use: when its provider cannot answer, the count and the send are refused (503) rather than reaching people the sender meant to leave out. Platform gate: the facets describe tenants across the platform. With no contribution, the composer offers no facet.

Which addresses another module already mails about the same maintenance moment, so a person gets ONE mail (an internal planning document B): asked before a maintenance notice of a tenant's window goes out by mail at its start or end, with the addresses it would mail. Default export: { coveredAddresses({ tenantId, windowId, stage: 'start' | 'end', emails }) => Promise<string[]> } (MailCoverageProvider in server/announcement.types.ts), a subset of `emails`, which the notice then leaves out of its mail (the bell, banner and toast still reach them). observability contributes its status-page subscribers, mailed at a window's start and end. Best-effort: a provider that fails covers nobody and the notice mails everyone it would.

A module publishes its OpenAPI 3.x document(s) to the API docs. Default export: { listDocuments(tenantId) } implementing OpenApiSourceProvider; each document is { key, document } where key matches ^[a-z0-9._-]{1,60}$ and document is plain OpenAPI JSON (at most 4 MB, treated as untrusted data and converted for the viewer, never executed). At most 5 documents per provider. A provider that throws is skipped and counted. api_doc imports nothing of the contributing module.

A strip above every admin page: something the person working here must know about the workspace or their own presence in it (maintenance in progress, a delegate's 'you are working here on behalf of…', fleet alerts). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'app_shell.banners': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'app_shell.banners', component, order, scope }; the maintenance strip (tenant, 0) comes first. Props received: { tenantId }. A contribution renders nothing when it has nothing to say, and must not fetch more than once per mount, because it sits on every admin page. The shell imports none of them (EXT-14).

A React context provider that the whole admin area must sit inside, mounted by the shell because the shell lives in a layout and so outlives navigation (the softphone: a call must survive moving between screens). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'app_shell.providers': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'app_shell.providers', component, order, scope: 'tenant' }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, children } that renders its children inside what it provides. Contributions nest in order, the first outermost; with none, the content renders unwrapped.

A control in the admin top bar, between the shell's own theme toggle and the user menu. Contributions sort by `order`: the call widget (telephony, 10) first, because a ringing telephone outranks a notification, then the unread-messages badge (messaging, 20) and the notification bell (notification_inapp, 30). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'app_shell.topbar': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'app_shell.topbar', component, order, scope }. Props received: { tenantId }. A contribution renders nothing when it has nothing to show, since it is on every admin page. The shell imports none of them (EXT-14).

The decision step of a queue item whose approval is more than a reviewer's click (a class 3 fleet command is approved by signing it with a security key). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'approval.item.decision': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'approval.item.decision', component, order, scope: 'tenant' }. Props received: { tenantId, item, onChanged } where item is the open queue item and onChanged reloads it. Every contribution renders nothing for an entityType that is not its own. The owner marks its items with metadata.decisionStep (a string); the queue then withholds its own Approve for them, and the owner registers a decision guard (ApprovalQueueService.registerDecisionGuard) so a bare APPROVE through the API is refused too.

Resolves a bare holder uuid to something a human reads. Default export: { holderType, getLabels(tenantId, holderIds) => Promise<Map<string,string>> }. Batched by contract — a 200-row register page must not become 200 lookups. `asset` cannot resolve holders itself without learning what an employee, a department and a customer are, which is the coupling the holderType/holderId seam exists to avoid. With no contributor the list falls back to `TYPE · <short id>`: honest rather than broken. Labels are keyed `TYPE:id` because two populations can legitimately share a uuid, and keying on the bare id would show one population's name against the other's row.

Asked before an asset is retired, disposed or deleted whether the contributing module still holds live rows pointing at it. Default export: (tenantId, assetId) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the change into a 409 naming the module. An open custody assignment is NOT this point's job — `AssetService.setStatus` already closes those itself, since that data belongs to `asset`. This is for rows `asset` cannot see, e.g. an open `field_service` order for the device. Mirrors `organization:reference_check`.

Where the rows of a retention purge are written before they are deleted. A contribution default-exports () => Promise<AuditArchiveExporter | null>: the exporter (export(tenantId, ndjson, rowCount)) when the destination is configured, null when it is not. No contribution, or null from every one, means no archive: the purge still proceeds and the chain stays provable through its checkpoint. A contribution that THROWS fails closed: the sweep skips the sealed tenants it would have archived instead of deleting rows an operator meant to keep. Only SEALED tenants are archived (a legacy row carries the actor id in the clear). The exporter must write the NDJSON it is given to a write-once destination and must not read it back. audit_log imports none of its providers.

A module that wants to hear every written audit row (an internal planning document §1.4a; the AI firewall's audit intake). Default export: { key?, actions?: string[], onRecord(record) } where record is the frozen WrittenAuditRecord { tenantId, action, severity, actorType, actorId, onBehalfOfActorId, actorTenantId, resourceType, resourceId, ipAddress, userAgent, metadata, nodeId, occurredAt, sealed }. `actions` narrows the subscription; a sink without it hears every row, say it out loud. Called AFTER the row's transaction committed, FIRE-AND-FORGET: log() sits on the path of every audited operation, so a sink that is slow, broken or missing must never delay or fail a write (a write that failed tells no sink). Each sink is isolated; a throw is logged and dropped. Actor ids travel in the clear (also for a sealed chain): a sink that stores what it hears covers that store with its own export and erasure contributions. A sink must not write an audit row for every row it hears (that loops). audit_log imports none of its sinks.

Modules contribute subject attribute resolvers (PIP): `(tenantId) => Promise<object>`, exposed to policies as `subject.<key>`. Loaded lazily by the PDP and ONLY when a loaded policy references the key; a failing or slow (2s) provider leaves the attribute absent (no opinion, never an accidental permit); a key that collides with a core subject attribute (id/role/roles/permissions/…) is refused.

Modules contribute record-level scope resolvers: given a tenant, a user and a permission id, return how wide that user's read is (OWN | TEAM | ALL) and, for TEAM, the opaque id set the caller turns into a predicate. FAIL-CLOSED, unlike every other provider point here: a throwing or timing-out provider yields OWN, because the failure mode of a missing scope predicate is not less data but all of it.

A national/government digital-identity (SAML or OIDC) provider implementation. Providers come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @turksat/edevlet, @esia/acs); the host resolves them per tenant through listExternalContributions, and trust-critical verification stays host-side. Provider descriptors and per-tenant config stay in the host's ACS_CATALOG / config service.

An OAuth/OIDC SSO provider implementation. Providers come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @google/sso, @github/sso); the host resolves them per tenant through listExternalContributions and keeps config and the client secret host-side.

Where 'this person agreed to this' is written. Default export: (event) => Promise<boolean> — return true when the event was recorded, false to let auth fall back. Events are either DOCUMENT (terms/privacy accepted at a named version — a registration consent has no content hash, and the ledger must not pretend otherwise) or PURPOSE (marketing/analytics granted or withdrawn). The point exists because terms_consent is the surviving ledger (DUP-03) but auth CANNOT hard-require it: a deployment that sells no agreements still has to register users (AGENTS.md §10). With no contributor, auth writes its own lightweight user_consents row exactly as before; with terms_consent installed, registration and JIT-SSO consents land in the same table as checkout acceptances instead of a parallel one nothing joins to. Best-effort by contract — a consent write must never block a signup.

Whether PEOPLE may hold and use credentials of this deployment (password login, registration, password reset and change, magic link, TOTP setup, passkey login and registration, and the node-local external identity providers: social SSO, tenant SAML, national identity and e-signature login, their JIT registration and Connected Accounts linking). Default export: () => Promise<{ allowed: boolean; reason?: string }>. Every contribution is asked; any refusal, and any contribution that throws, times out or is paused, blocks local credentials (fail closed: the guard only exists where people log in elsewhere). No contribution = allowed, as before. auth answers 403 LOCAL_CREDENTIALS_DISABLED. Exists so auth never imports the fleet: fleet_agent answers it on a node whose region requires Fleet ID (FID-07, decision F15). Break-glass shadow operators do not pass through it.

An alternative sign-in method on the login page (passkey, e-signature, ...). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'auth.login.methods': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'auth.login.methods', component, order, scope: 'tenant' } and the page resolves it through the generated client component map. Props received: { tenantId, onSuccess(message) } — the contribution supplies its own success wording, because the module owning the method is the one that knows what it is called. Declared so `auth` never imports an authentication satellite: auth is PROTECTED and always installed, so a static import forced every optional method module on with it, and auth_e_signature requires auth back (MIS-01, audit 2026-08).

Extra named sections a satellite adds to the 'who am I' answer (GET /auth/session and the device login body). Default export: ({ tenantId, userId }) => Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null>; each key of the returned object becomes a top-level field. Reserved fields (user, tenant, tenantMember, userSecurity, tokens) cannot be overwritten. Best-effort by contract: a failing contribution is skipped. Exists so auth never imports a satellite — terms_consent contributes `compliance.pendingAgreements` (required agreements not yet accepted at their current version) without auth knowing it exists (AGENTS.md §10).

Whether a sign-up that the fleet instance's zone chooser sent here (`/auth/onboarding?fleet=1&zone=<id>`) may open a workspace on THIS deployment, and the language it starts with (an internal planning document, F41). Default export: (zoneId: string) => Promise<{ ok: true; zoneId; domain; defaultLocale } | { ok: false; reason; chooserUrl }>. Asked only on a fleet node; no contribution = the zone means nothing here. Any refusal, and any contribution that throws, times out or is paused, refuses the sign-up (fail closed). Exists so auth never imports the fleet: fleet_agent answers it from the installed trust bundle.

A second-factor method for the request-bound step-up (P9-19, auth.step-up.ts), selected by key; auth_passkey contributes `webauthn`. Default export: { available({ userId }), begin({ userId }) => { options, state }, verify({ userId, state, response }) => boolean }: `begin` answers the authenticator options and an opaque state (the challenge) auth keeps with its own single-use challenge; `verify` must answer true only for an assertion by a credential of that user, made with user verification, over that state. A method that is not installed, switched off or failing is simply not offered (TOTP, built into auth, is the fallback); one that disappears between options and verify fails the step-up closed (503). Exists so auth never imports auth_passkey, which requires auth (AGENTS.md §9.2).

A named choice list for source fields. Default export: { name, list(tenantId, query), resolve?(tenantId, ids), byName?(tenantId, names), entityType?, ownerOf?(tenantId, id), requiredPermission? }. Contributed lists are <prefix>.<list>; unprefixed names are reserved for automation. A provider returns only the tenant's rows. Each contribution lists its list names in metadata.ids, and two contributions listing one name fail the registry snapshot.

A config node type (a connection or credential set referenced by nodes). Default export: { type, declaration, secretFields, provides?, test?(tenantId, values) }. Secrets are substituted host-side at call time and never enter a message, trace, log or export. Each contribution lists its config types in metadata.ids, and two contributions listing one type fail the registry snapshot.

A module that builds flows from its own records and keeps them (owned flows, an internal planning document 1.3). Default export: { key, label(locale), editHint(locale), limitKey, detach?(tenantId, flowId, ownerRef) }; the type is FlowOwnerContribution in registry/flow-owner.types.ts. key is the contributing module's id and its only metadata.ids entry; two contributions listing one key fail the registry snapshot. The module deploys its flows with the server-only DeployInternalOptions.owner = { module: key, ref }; the engine runs them like any flow, but people cannot change them through the flow API (409 owned_flow naming the label), they are left out of max_flows (the owner counts them against limitKey), and the editor opens them read-only with editHint and a one-way Detach (automation.manage and max_flows headroom), which calls detach under the tenant's deploy lock (it must not deploy) and then makes the flow ordinary. A refused contribution is logged and skipped; its flows stay locked until detached.

Where flows run. Default export: the AutomationHost descriptor (key, label, msgTypes, systemMetadata, entryScopes, capabilities, testRunner, limits?, foreignTypes?, partitions). A duplicate key fails the registry; a flow whose host is not installed shows host_missing and cannot be deployed.

A node type. Default export: a NodeContribution or an array of them ({ type, declaration, executor, migrations?, hosts?, outputsFor?, ready?, deployCheck?, external?, barrier?, safeRead?, lookup?, parallel?, timeout?, breaker?, stateful?, holds?, originatorRewrite? }; the types are NodeContribution in registry/node.types.ts). The declaration is the router's blocks.d shape plus version, mutates, async, whenMissing, runtimes, help and sample. Loaded without the tenant filter, so a disabled contributor's nodes still render ready:false and its executors are never called; an invalid contribution is logged and skipped. Each contribution lists its node types in metadata.ids, and two contributions listing one type fail the registry snapshot. Naming: the router-shared families trigger|cond|logic|action|enrich keep their names; a business module's own node is <module>.<verb>.

A custom param editor for one node type: { type, Editor }, with the type also in the entry's metadata.type so CI can check it without React. The generated form is used when a type has none. A custom editor never widens what the API accepts: the server validates the declaration's params.

Counts what references a flow, for delete guards. Default export: (tenantId, flowId) => Promise<{ count, label }>. A check that fails to load or throws blocks the delete (references cannot be verified). Unlike the hr / asset / organization reference checks, an answer of null or undefined also counts as 'cannot answer' and blocks the delete, so a contributor with no references returns { count: 0, label }. Zero contributors are expected until a module outside automation stores an automation flow id (none does today; an internal planning document); until then a delete checks only automation's own references (other flows, root bindings).

A seed flow offered on a host. Default export: { key, host, title, description, flow, seed? } where flow is a roltek-automation-1 flow of known node types. Each contribution lists its template keys in metadata.ids, and two contributions listing one key fail the registry snapshot.

BOOKABILITY CONSTRAINTS, not availability answers (Layer C). Default export: { scopeTypes?, getConstraints(tenantId, { scopeTypes }) => Promise<AvailabilityConstraint | null> } where the constraint may set slotMinutes, stepMinutes, leadTimeMinutes, horizonDays, capacity, bufferMinutes. CalendarService remains the single resolver: open hours minus holidays minus busy occurrences, narrowed by these constraints, produces the slots. Every field NARROWS and the strictest value wins, which is what makes merging several contributors well-defined without a precedence scheme — and precedence would need an owner, which is the ownership this point was inverted to avoid. This contract was inverted on 2026-08-02 and IMPLEMENTED in W2.5; it previously read 'a provider that returns what is bookable', which would have made the first booking module the owner of availability logic.

The PULL side of busy time (Layer C). Default export: { subjectTypes?, getBusy(tenantId, { subjects, from, to }) => Promise<Array<{ start, end, busyStatus?, title? }>> }. Occurrences owned inside this deployment are WRITTEN THROUGH into calendar_events instead, so free/busy stays one indexed range scan; this point is for sources that genuinely cannot push — an external ICS feed, a third-party calendar, a legacy system. Direction is deliberate: contributors report BUSY, calendar computes availability. Providers run concurrently. A provider that throws contributes NOTHING and is logged, which makes time look FREE that may not be — the unsafe direction, taken because failing the whole query makes the calendar unusable whenever a third party is down. Pass strictBusySources to refuse instead.

Display-only items a domain wants rendered as a toggleable layer on the calendar surface (invoices falling due, orders shipping this week, subscription renewals). Default export: { key, label, requiredPermission?, getItems(tenantId, { from, to, filters }) => Promise<FeedItem[]> } where FeedItem is { id, title, at, endsAt?, href?, badge? }. Resolved by calendar.feed.ts and served by GET /api/calendar/feed. Items are query-time: NEVER materialised as occurrences and never part of free/busy — this is the answer to 'everything with a timestamp should be visible on the calendar' that does not turn the occurrence store into a log table. If a human plans or reviews their time with it, it is an occurrence or a projection; if they merely want to see it on the time axis, it is a feed. `requiredPermission` is the CONTRIBUTOR's permission and is checked per layer, because the surface itself only asks for calendar.events.read and a feed carries the contributor's own data. A provider that throws contributes nothing and is reported: an absent layer costs a reader context, unlike a failing busy_source, which silently makes time look free. Declared with a bare-function contract until 2026-09-08; a toggleable layer needs a key and a name, so the implemented contract is the object above.

A country/region holiday pack, keyed by lowercase ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 ('tr', 'de', 'fr'). Default export: (tenantId, year) => Promise<BuiltinHoliday[]> — pure data, never a database write. Resolved by HolidayCalendarService.seedFromBuiltin so calendar never imports a country pack. The Turkish pack ships in-tree (server/data/holidays.tr.data.ts) as the built-in default; a contributed 'tr' pack overrides it.
A CAPTCHA verification backend (reCAPTCHA / hCaptcha / Turnstile). Sandboxed community plugins (the captcha plugin family) contribute their token-verification here.

Invoked after a committed cart lifecycle change. Default export: (tenantId, evt: { event: 'ABANDONED', cartId, userId, email, currency, itemCount, subtotalMinor, recoveryAllowed }) => Promise<void>. Awaited, each contribution inside its OWN try/catch, so a broken satellite never fails the sweep. marketing sends its CART_ABANDONED triggered campaigns from here (commerce plan 02 §7.2).

Invoked after a committed product or variant deletion. Default export: (tenantId, evt: { event: 'PRODUCT_DELETED', productId } | { event: 'VARIANT_DELETED', productId, variantId }) => Promise<void>. Deletion is terminal (soft delete, no restore path), so a module holding references to products (wishlist items) may drop them outright. Each contribution runs in its own try/catch and a failing hook never fails the deletion. The edge points consumer to catalogue; the catalogue imports none of its listeners.

Supplies sellable on-hand quantity for catalog products/variants. Default export: (tenantId, items: Array<{ productId, variantId? }>) => Promise<Map<string, number>> keyed 'productId' or 'productId:variantId'. OMIT an item you know nothing about — an absent key falls back to the product's flat stockQuantity column, a 0 means 'none in stock'. Declared so the catalog never imports inventory: a storefront-only tenant with no inventory module keeps selling. inventory contributes from inventory_stock_items; the old warehouseStock jsonb this replaced was dropped in migration 014.

A step a process runs at boot: registering an in-process hook or an approval decision handler, or scheduling a recurring job and starting its queue consumer. Contribute with `key` (the task name with underscores), `export` (the file that holds the function), `order` (the sequence across modules), and `metadata`: `phase` ('guard' runs first in every process and is a precondition of serving: a guard that throws stops the process before anything else starts; 'runtime' always runs, right after the guards, for in-process hooks such as the server-message overlay; 'approval' always runs; 'consumer' starts a delivery queue consumer and always runs; 'scheduler' runs only where ENABLE_BACKGROUND_JOBS=true), `fn` (the exported function to call, with no arguments), `name` (the name used in boot logs) and, for a scheduler, optionally `parallel: true`: by default a scheduler task is single-owner work and runs in exactly one process of the cluster (the holder of the `proc:leader:<kind>:schedulers` lock, an internal planning document task 2) when the process passes a leader runner; `parallel` tasks (a queue consumer, a host that shares its work through leases) run in every process. Each task runs in its own try, so a task that throws is logged and the rest still start. Read by common/server/boot-tasks.ts; there is no list of modules anywhere in the boot path.

Why a contributing module may not run for a tenant (an internal planning document). Default export: ContributorStateSource { states(tenantId) => Promise<StateVerdict[]> }, listing only the modules the source objects to, each with a state (disabled, uninstalled, unentitled, blocked, retired, banned, quarantined, missing) and a reason an admin can read. Read by common/server/extensions with no gating of its own; the most severe state per module wins. A failing source falls back to its last good answer, else it is ignored and logged.

A panel on a record's page that another module adds: the activity log, tags, tasks, a gallery, SEO. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'common.entity.panels': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'common.entity.panels', component, order, props: { panelId, region: 'main' | 'side' | 'tab', entityTypes: ['*'] or the subject types it serves, title, titleKey } }. The record's page renders <EntityPanels region> and useEntityPanelTabs() (common/ui/entity-panels.component) and may exclude a panel id or pass it page props; a panel receives { tenantId, entityType, entityId } plus those. The page imports and requires none of the contributors (EXT-14), and a panel whose module is off leaves no frame.

Which days are public holidays for a tenant, for modules that schedule around holidays without owning a calendar (on_call's holiday-aware rotation restrictions). Default export: HolidayLookup { datesBetween(tenantId, from, to) => 'YYYY-MM-DD'[] } (inclusive, calendar days in the tenant's holiday calendars). The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, no day is a holiday. Hosted by `common` so that calendar can serve on_call without a contribution cycle (on_call contributes to calendar:feed).

Who a bare user id is, for modules that store one without owning people (loyalty's accounts list: find a member by name or e-mail, show the member's name). Default export: MemberLookup { search(tenantId, text, { limit }) => MemberRef[]; resolve(tenantId, userIds) => MemberRef[] }, MemberRef = { userId, name | null, email | null }. Only the tenant's ACTIVE members, never another tenant's people; search answers at most 25, resolve takes at most 200 ids. Read through common/server/common.member-lookup (searchMembers, resolveMembers), which answer nobody when no contribution is active or it fails, so the consumer shows the bare id. tenant_member contributes it. Hosted by `common` so a consumer of any edition reads members without requiring tenant_member or user. The e-mail is shown only behind an admin-level permission.

Prices a basket of references against price lists and rules, for modules that show prices without owning price lists (the shop catalog). Default export: an object with resolve(tenantId, { currency, customer?, lines }) returning [{ reference, unitPriceMinor, currency }] (the shape is PriceResolver in commerce_catalog/server/commerce_catalog.pricing.service.ts). The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, prices are the base prices. Hosted by `common` so that the module that shows prices and the one that resolves them can contribute to each other without a contribution cycle.

Whose installed plugin providers serve a tenant at a host point (an internal planning document, 53.4): 'own' (the tenant's installs and secrets), 'root' (the root tenant's installs, run in the tenant's scope with the root tenant's secrets and plugin config) or 'own_then_root' (the tenant's own when one is configured, else the root tenant's). Default export: ProviderScopeSource { scope(tenantId, point) => ProviderScope | null }, null for a point no setting level covers. Read by common/server/external-extensions (listExternalContributions) only for points a module's setting level lists; no answer or a failing one is 'own', which never hands out the root tenant's secrets. Platform gate: the level is the operator's choice, not a feature the tenant switches. Hosted by `common` because the level lives in tenant_setting, which imports `common`.

An automated phone call that reads a text aloud and waits for a key press, for modules that page people by voice without owning a telephony stack. Default export: ScriptedCallApi { available(tenantId), place({ tenantId, to, text, handler: { key, token }, party: { type, id }, idempotencyKey? }) } (telephony's scripted-call service). The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, the voice channel is unavailable. Hosted by `common` so that telephony can serve on_call without a contribution cycle (on_call contributes to telephony:scripted_call_handler).

The tenant's own origin (https://acme.example.com) for links that leave the app: mails, push payloads, webhook bodies. Default export: TenantOriginSource { origin(tenantId) => string | null }, null when the tenant has no origin that serves (path mode, no live domain). Read by common/server/tenant-url (absoluteTenantUrl, tenantOrigin), which falls back to the platform host's /tenant/{id} form (platformTenantUrl). Platform gate (since 2026-10-17, was behaviour): every tenant keeps a free <slug>.<wildcard> subdomain, which is the platform's routing of the tenant and not a feature it switches on, so tenant_domain answers for every tenant whose module is in the build and not banned or retired. Which domain it answers (a custom domain only while it is ACTIVE and the plan includes custom domains, otherwise the free subdomain) is tenant_domain's decision, not the gate's. Hosted by `common` so every module that mails a link builds it without importing tenant_domain, which requires most of them back.

Where a module records metered usage without owning the metering store. Default export: UsageMeterSink { ensureMeter(tenantId, { key, name, unit }), record(tenantId, { meterKey, quantity, idempotencyKey?, metadata? }) }. The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, usage is not recorded (the callers are best-effort by design). Read by common/server/common.usage-meter (loadUsageMeterSink) for observability's probe, alert, telemetry and query meters and on_call's page, SMS and voice meters. The 30 s budget covers the cold load of the metering service in a fresh process. Hosted by `common` so that metering (Enterprise) can serve Core callers with one contribution and no contribution cycle.
One country's registry. Answers whether a recipient may be contacted, and — where the law requires pre-registration — records them.

Answers whether a caller may see one record of the contributing module, for a party an outbound message is attached to. Default export: { partyType, canSee(tenantId, userId, partyId) => Promise<boolean> }. The outbound-email route writes a timeline row against the party, so a party of a type contact does not own (CRM_LEAD, CRM_OPPORTUNITY, ...) is checked here: it must exist in the tenant and be inside the caller's record scope. FAIL-CLOSED: no contributor for the party type, a contributor that fails or does not answer, or false is the same 404 as a missing record (activity.02).

The domain-specific half of an agreement. Default export: { contractTypes?, getTerms(tenantId, contractId) => Promise<ContractTermsSection[]> }. `contract` holds only what every agreement has; a salary, a delivery SLA or a licence seat count belongs to the consumer, in the consumer's own table, and this point is how the contract surface shows it anyway. The direction is what keeps the narrow pass honest: pulling those fields onto the contract row would make it the union of every agreement anyone has. Providers run concurrently and a failure costs that section, not the page — a broken HR extension must not make a procurement framework unreadable.

Modules expose their records that ended up with no owner, plus a `claim` callback. The sweep decides who should own a record and the owning module performs the write, because only it knows what else that implies.

Invoked after a committed lead write. Default export: (tenantId, evt: { event: 'CREATED', leadId, name, email, source }) => Promise<void>. Awaited, each contribution inside its OWN try/catch, so a broken satellite can never fail a lead. marketing fires its CRM_LEAD_CREATED triggered campaigns from here.

The "More actions" menu of the stored diagram editor (dashboard phase 50: "Make a 3D view of this drawing"). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'dashboard_scada.diagram_editor.menu': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'dashboard_scada.diagram_editor.menu', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, diagramId, diagramName, register, layer } that draws nothing and registers its entries with register(item) (the kit's SceneEditorMenuItem: id, label, onSelect({ dirty }), disabled?, disabledReason?), which answers the function that takes the entry away. layer is the editor's own element (null until drawn): a dialog an entry opens mounts there (ConfirmDialog portalTarget), since the full-screen editor covers body-level dialogs. The editor renders the slot only when the contributing module is on and the viewer holds its permissions, each contribution isolated in an error boundary; with none, the editor has no menu. dashboard_scada imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

The card menu of a process diagram card (`scada.scene`), dashboard phase 42.5.4 (phase 46.3: "Open <name>'s views", the link to the subject's Views, replaced "Set up scene…"), with "Edit symbols" and its side panel for the subject of the page the card is on, in the slot the card draws and the diagram kind (the pattern of `viewer.design`'s). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'dashboard_scada.card.scene_setup': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'dashboard_scada.card.scene_setup', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { kind: 'diagram' } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, slot } (plus its manifest props) and registers its menu entries with `useCardMenuEntry` (dashboard/ui/card-menu) and draws the side panel. The 2D card renders the slot next to itself, only when the contributing module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set), each contribution isolated in an error boundary; nothing is drawn without one. dashboard_scada imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

The read-only preview of a scene kind in the Scene drawer, dashboard phase 42.5.4: the chosen document drawn with a click on an item answering with its scene key ("Pick"), and, by being contributed at all, the kind is offered in the drawer's kind choice. The design kind is this module's own; the 2D `diagram` kind's is dashboard_scada's. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'dashboard_viewer.scene_setup.preview': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'dashboard_viewer.scene_setup.preview', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { kind } }, the permissions being the kind's own read and write; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, documentId, selected, onPick } (plus its manifest props: `selected` is the key to outline, `onPick(key)` takes the key a click chose). The drawer offers a kind only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions, and isolates each preview in an error boundary. dashboard_viewer imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

A module contributes board templates (an internal planning document). Default export: one BoardTemplate or an array. BoardTemplate = { key, title, description?, anchor: { workspace } | { moduleId }, sections?: [{ title, countableKeys }] | placements?: [{ widgetRef, x, y, w, h, title?, settings?, dataBinding? (DataBindingSchema, `{ $param }` allowed), refreshSeconds?, actions?, pageKey?, fallback? }], timeWindow?, params? (value and entity parameters, phase 41), pages?, mainPage?, titleKey?, descriptionKey?, ask? } — a template has sections OR placements. Every placement is validated by the same schemas a manual placement passes and re-resolved for the applying caller; one the caller cannot see is replaced by its `fallback` card (phase 49b: another widget on the same cells and page) when the caller can place that one, else skipped and reported by name. `ask` (phase 49b) is the one question a person answers when the New dashboard dialog makes a board of its own from the template (`apply` with `asNew`): which entities one of its entity parameters of many holds (`all` as declared, `subtype` one subtype of its type, `under` the entities under one entity of the type through a relations provider); the answer is stored as that parameter's choice. `titleKey`, `descriptionKey` and each question text's `labelKey` name the contributor's dictionary keys, so the gallery and the dialog say them in the viewer's language. A template that asks is never placed onto another board. A template of a disabled module disappears from the gallery; an invalid one, or one reusing a key, is logged and skipped, built-ins win collisions. The dashboard never names a contributor.

A command a widget can fire (an internal planning document §12.7, OD-80). Default export: { label, paramsSchema (FieldSchema map), requiredPermission, confirm?: 'none'|'confirm'|'typed', confirmText?, execute(ctx: { tenantId, userId, locale }, params) => Promise<{ ok: true, value? } | void> }. Resolved by the contribution `key` and run ONLY through POST /api/dashboard/commands/[key] for a placement configured with a `command` action: the runner enforces the placement, the command's own permission BEFORE execute(), the confirmation policy, params validation (unknown keys rejected), a once-only `requestId` (replay guard) and writes an audit row per attempt (ok / error / denied / rejected). A command that takes a resource id must authorise that resource itself in execute(); a `command` action can only be saved by someone holding the command's permission. The dashboard module knows no domain concept; a command throws AppError to refuse.

One stat-card-worthy count. A module default-exports an ARRAY of DashboardCountable ({ key, label, requiredPermission, count(tenantId) }); the first-party entity_count data source turns each into a permission-gated scalar query named <moduleId>.<key>. Counts arrive by contribution, never by URL or table name.

A server module answering named, parameterised queries for widgets (phase 4b). Contribution `key` = the source key a binding names. THERE IS NO URL IN THIS MODEL — a widget names (sourceKey, queryKey, params) and the runner closes all three: the key must resolve in the build-time map, the query must appear in describe(), params validate against the query's FieldSchema with unknown keys rejected. Every query declares its own requiredPermission (enforced by the runner BEFORE execute()) and an explicit cacheScope ('tenant' | 'user' — required; the wrong one leaks one member's data to another).

The commands a widget kind lets its ELEMENTS run (an internal planning document, task 28.1). The element gestures (elementClick, elementDoubleClick, elementContextClick) are part of the dashboard's action model; what an element is (a symbol of a process diagram) belongs to the widget. `key` = a manifest key, `metadata.widgetType` = the widget type served (a key cannot hold a dot); the default export is an ElementActionsProvider { allowsCommands(settings), validateEntries(settings, entries), keepsEntries(settings, stored), hasElement(settings, elementKey), confirmFloor(entry), auditFields(entry) }, all pure. The DTO checks the SHAPE of a command entry on an element gesture; instance create/update (422) and the run route (404) ask the provider of the placement's widget type. No provider for the type, or its module off for the tenant: commands on the widget's elements are refused. The generic command gates (permission, rate limit, replay, the audit row) stay in the dashboard; `confirmFloor` is added to the command's own confirmation policy and `auditFields` to the audit row.

A relation graph board aliases can walk (an internal planning document, the relations query and the entity search query). Contribution `key` = the provider an alias names (`iot_asset`). Default export: DashboardEntityRelations { key, label(locale), requiredPermission, relationTypes(ctx), query(ctx, { root, direction, maxLevel 1..10, lastLevelOnly, filters, limit }), holds? } returning typed entity refs; the dashboard names them through the contributed entity types (so each type's read permission still applies) and caps the set at 500. `holds` (optional, phase 49b): entity type -> the entity types it holds through CONTAINS in this graph; a card slot handed an entity of another kind (D112) walks only the graphs that say that kind holds one of the slot's types, and the card's picker offers such a parameter only then (a graph that declares nothing may hold anything).

An entity kind board aliases can select (an internal planning document, E36-2). Contribution `key` = the entity type an alias names (`iot_device`). The default export is a DashboardEntityType { key, labels(locale), requiredPermission, subtypes?(ctx, q), byIds(ctx, ids), find(ctx, { subtypes?, namePrefix?, search?, limit }) }: the dashboard keeps the generic filter types (single, list, name, type, state, subtype) and asks the module for the entities, never reading its tables. The resolver asks the viewer for `requiredPermission` before any call; the module reads in the tenant's RLS transaction with an explicit tenant predicate, so another tenant's id is an unknown id. Persists: a board stores the key in its aliases.

Code the widget kit loads on demand, and the lock state of the kit's options, contributed by a module that adds content to a builtin kind (an internal planning document, contract C3). CLIENT contribution; the default export is a KitRuntimeDefinition { loaders: { <the kit's key>: () => import(...) }, useOptionLocks?({ tenantId, enabled }) -> { <option value>: { locked: true, offer? } } | null }, resolved through the generated client map (common/ui/generated/module-dashboard-kit-runtime.ts). Every kit host (`useKitHost`: a board's cards, a display screen, the settings editor) installs into the kit (common/ui/kui/widget-kit/kit-runtime.ts) the definitions of the modules active for the tenant and removes the others' (`kit-runtime.registry.ts`, the `_MODULES` + useExtensionActive pattern of dashboard:placement_editor), so a tenant without the module never has its loaders and never downloads that code. The kit calls a loader the first time it needs that code. A locked option is shown and kept but not newly added; no contribution, or null locks, means every option is open. A lock may carry `title` (why, in the viewer's language), `offer` (what opens it, with a link) and `picture` (the kit key of a loader that resolves to static pictures by option value, drawn instead of the option's own drawing, so a locked option loads none of its code). A kit part that shows locks says so (`wantKitOptionLocks`), so a contribution can wait for that before working them out. Outside any scope every definition is installed.

Which marketplace listings may show for a tenant, so a board drops the widgets of a paused or revoked plugin. Each provider vouches for its own part: plugin_runtime for switched on, marketplace for not revoked (taken down, version withdrawn or yanked, publisher suspended, unpaid, blocked by policy). A listing shows only when every provider includes it; with no provider, or one that fails, none does. Default export: { activeListingIds(tenantId, listingIds) => Promise<Set<string>> } (ListingActivityProvider in server/dashboard.listing-activity.ts).

A widget kind's own full-screen editor (the process diagram's canvas), contributed by the module that owns the kind (an internal planning document, task 28.1). CLIENT contribution: `metadata` = { widgetType, label (English default) }; the default export is a PlacementEditorDefinition { widgetType, label(t), icon?, Component, elementSources?, elementDocument?, runtime? } resolved through the generated client map (common/ui/generated/module-dashboard-placement-editor.ts). The settings drawer and the board's customise mode (toolbar, right-click menu, narrow list) offer an action labelled `label` on a card of that type and open `Component` over the page with PlacementEditorProps { tenantId, placementId, title, settings, binding, boardParams, drafts (the editor edits its own copy), columns?, onApply(settings, drafts) -> { ok: true } | { ok: false, message? }, onClose }. `elementSources(t, settings, document?)` are the element-gesture sources the drawer edits for the type; `elementDocument` { setting, read(tenantId, id) } names the setting that holds a stored document the card draws (the process diagram's own drawing) and the kind's own reader of it: the drawer reads it while the setting holds an id and hands it to `elementSources`, so the gestures name that document's elements (phase 52.5.4); `runtime` is a hook (PlacementRuntimeHook) BuiltinPlacement calls for every card of the type: it returns the data the card draws (e.g. pending / failed rows overlaid), an action-context patch (runEntryCommand), the view's extra props (elementActions) and a dialog. A definition of a module that is not active for the tenant is not offered; with none, nothing changes for the type.

What a placement of a builtin widget kind may hold for a tenant, judged by the module that limits it (an internal planning document, contract C4). `metadata.types` lists the builtin kind types a contribution guards; the default export is a PlacementGuard ({ tenantId, widgetType, settings, previous }) => Promise<void> (server/placement-guard.types.ts). The dashboard asks the guards of the kind after template validation on every write that stores its settings: a placement create and update, a template apply and a board import (createMany), the cards a board is laid out with (materialize), a board copy (each card a new placement), a preset's create, an edit of its defaults and its publish. `settings` and `previous` are the kind's EFFECTIVE settings (template defaults, a preset's defaults, the stored object, upgraded); `previous` is null when nothing is stored to compare with. A guard refuses by throwing an AppError below 500: the write is answered 422 with `details.reason` = `placement_guard_refused` (the guard's own reason in `details.guardReason`), which a board copy and an import rethrow instead of swallowing. Anything else a guard throws, a guard that cannot be loaded or answer in time: 503 `placement_guard_unavailable`, nothing stored (fails closed). Guards run in order and the first refusal stops the rest. Only contributions of modules active for the tenant run; a type no contribution lists loads nothing. The dashboard names no contributor and no kind.

Renders the sandboxed iframe of a community plugin's widget on a board. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'dashboard.plugin_frame': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'dashboard.plugin_frame', component, order, scope: 'tenant' }. Props received: { tenantId, listingId }. The board renders it only for a widget of render tier `iframe`; with no contribution that widget shows nothing.

A kind of document a scene binding can name (an internal planning document, D42-3): `design` (a 3D design, from dashboard_viewer), `diagram` (a 2D process diagram, from dashboard_scada). Contribution `key` = the kind a binding stores. The default export is a DashboardSceneKind { key, list(ctx, { search?, limit }), byIds(ctx, ids) -> [{ id, name, hash }], keysOf(ctx, id) -> [{ key, label, kind }], readPermission, writePermission }: the dashboard keeps the binding table, the routes and the resolver and asks the module for the documents, never reading its tables. A binding is written with the kind's `writePermission`, listed and used ("who uses this document") with its `readPermission`, both asked for the caller before any call. The module reads in the tenant's RLS transaction with an explicit tenant predicate, so another tenant's id is an unknown id. Persists: a binding stores the key.

A satellite module contributes a dashboard widget by default-exporting a WidgetDefinition (see ui/widget.types.ts). The COMPONENT travels through the generated client map modules/common/ui/generated/module-dashboard-widget.ts; the catalog metadata (workspace, size, order, permissions) travels in the contribution's `metadata`, because widget-catalog.service.ts is server code and that map is client code with static React imports. Use this only when contributing into a dashboard your module does not own — a module placing its OWN widget should use the simpler module.json `widgets[]` array. Contract: docs/marketplace-widget-seam.md is the third-party path; this is the in-tree one.

A module contributes a widget category (an internal planning document, decision D1) -- the second source of the category registry next to the four core ones (Charts, Data, Content, Controls). Default export: ONE { key, label, icon?, order? } or an ARRAY of them; key is the value stored in dashboard_widgets.category (letters, digits, space, & _ -; max 64), icon is a Font Awesome class, order is 100-999 (core occupies 10-40). Contributions appear only while the contributing module is enabled; an invalid one, or one reusing a taken key (core wins, then lower order), is logged and skipped. The registry orders the picker tabs and is the write-time allow-list for a widget's category; a stored value outside it stays readable and shows under Other. The dashboard knows no device or telemetry concept -- an IoT module contributes its own categories here.

Which module sells a product GROUP of the builtin widget KINDS (an internal planning document, tasks 28.1 and 28.3). The widget kit tags a builtin kind with an optional `group` (BuiltinKindSpec.group; scada.symbol and scada.scene carry `scada`); a module that sells the group contributes with `key` = the group id. `metadata` is documentation only: { category (the picker category the kinds are filed under), types? (the kind types, for a reader) }; nothing decides by `types`. One part is read, while the group is active (phase 42.5): the scene a kind of the group draws, as `sceneType` (the kind), `sceneKind`, `sceneDocumentSetting` and `sceneOwnedSettings`, the keys an `ext:` widget declares it with; the board open resolves such a card's scene and the overlay write path refuses its owned settings. A grouped kind is available to a tenant only while a contributor of its group is ACTIVE for it: with no contributor at all (the module is not in the build) or only an inactive one (switched off, not licensed), the catalogue read (picker, library) leaves it out, a placement create or update, a preset of it and its publish are refused with 422 WIDGET_KIND_UNAVAILABLE, and a stored placement stays intact and renders an inert 'not available' card. A kind without a group is never gated. The default export is the same record (WidgetKindGroup). Read from the contributions' static records only (no code is loaded); an unreadable module state blocks nothing.

What a module offers to be importable into. Default export: { key, label, fields(), apply(tenantId, rows, opts) => ImportApplyResult, undo?(tenantId, ref) }. The pipeline owns parsing, mapping, review, counters and undo; the TARGET owns validation and writes — data_import never interprets a row error, because a second validator disagreeing with the real one is worse than none. `apply` MUST honour opts.mode: a DRY_RUN that writes is the single most damaging bug this seam can carry. On APPLY the `refs` map is REQUIRED — it is the only thing undo reads, and an UPDATE without a `before` pre-image is counted as not-undoable rather than half-undone.

An idempotent data-upkeep step another module runs on EVERY deploy of the control database, such as dashboard publishing the platform's builtin widgets into the root tenant. Default export: PostDeployStep { run(ctx: PostDeployContext) => Promise<string | void> } (db.post-deploy.ts); ctx gives a DataSource on the deploy target (direct connection, the application's entities), withTenantTransaction(tenantId, fn(manager)) and log(message). Run one after another in extension order by deployDatabase after the bootstrap seed and the fleet tenant, under the deploy advisory lock. Not for the dedicated tenant databases of the fan-out, unless the contribution declares metadata { tenantDatabases: true }: the fan-out then also runs it against each dedicated tenant database after that database migrated cleanly (only the opted-in steps; such a step must not assume control-database tables). A step must be idempotent and must reach the database only through ctx (never the runtime DataSource, Redis or the env module: the deploy runs at build time and in a migrate sidecar). Best effort: a step that fails to load or throws is logged and reported in the deploy report's postDeploy, the others still run and the deploy does not fail. The 30 s budget covers loading the contribution; db never imports the owner.

A module that is not part of the seed runner's static list contributes its demo-data seeder here (an add-on package such as dashboard_scada: the runner is Enterprise, an add-on may not be imported from it, ADR-0013). Default export: SeederContribution { name, tier, deps?, run(ctx: SeedContext) } (db.seed-contracts.ts), the same entry the runner's own SEEDERS list holds; `run` is the module's `seed<Module>` function. The seed module reads the active contributions of the seeded tenant (a module that is off or not entitled for the tenant is not seeded) and runs them in their tier with the built-in seeders; the seeder names and tiers are checked together with the built-in ones. db never imports the contributor and never runs a seeder itself.

The columns a tenant data key (TDEK, P7-TDEK, decision F16) protects. The module that owns a tenant-scoped table contributes, next to its entity and in the same commit as the code that encrypts them, a default export `TENANT_KEY_COLUMNS: Array<{ table, idColumn, tenantColumn?, columns, rowFilter?: { column, values }, family, blindIndexes?: Array<{ column, of, purpose }>, skipValues? }>` (db.tenant-key-columns.ts): text columns that hold field-encryption v2 envelopes under the row tenant's key (db.tenant-keys.service.ts). db resolves, the owner contributes - db never imports the owner. The declarations drive the online re-encryption backfill, the `encryption.tdek_enabled` judge and the key-protected families of the deletion receipt; a ratchet test requires every secret- or special-category-patterned column of a tenant-scoped table to be declared here or waived with a reason. Every installed contribution counts whatever a tenant's module state (the declaration describes the schema).

A module declares append-only, time-keyed tables as time-series: default export is `TIME_SERIES_TABLES: Array<{ table, timeColumn, chunkInterval, retention?, compressAfter?, segmentBy?, tenantColumn?, continuousAggregates?, rollups? }>` (see db.time-series.ts). db resolves, the owning module contributes - db never imports the owner. With TimescaleDB the table becomes a hypertable with chunk-drop retention (TSL: policies, compression, continuous aggregates); without it the same declaration yields a plain table with a BRIN time index, a (tenantId, time DESC) btree and batched-delete retention. `rollups` (tenant-scoped tables) create tenant-isolated rollup tables (RLS + FORCE) filled per tenant by job `db-time-series-rollup`; an RLS hypertable cannot be compressed or feed a continuous aggregate, so those two are refused there. Every unique index/primary key of the entity MUST include the time column and, for a tenant-scoped table, START with the tenant column (e.g. `(tenantId, deviceId, keyId, ts)`: a key without the tenant lets a unique violation reveal another tenant's row; `ensureTimeSeriesTables` enforces it on the live table), and the (tenantId, time DESC) index is created in both modes.

Tells the access lattice who the caller is relative to a document: which owner rows they ARE (subjectOf), which owner populations they administer (custodianOf), and which owner rows they supervise (supervisorOf). Default export: { resolve(tenantId, { userId, tenantRole }) }. All three are domain knowledge `document` cannot compute — only HR knows who reports to whom. Contributions are merged by UNION and can only ever widen, so merge order is irrelevant and a broken guard removes access rather than granting it. With no contributor installed a caller is none of the three and the lattice denies by default.

Resolves bare owner uuids to display names for the vault list, a single document and the retention screen. Default export: { ownerType, getLabels(tenantId, ownerIds) => Promise<Map<string,string>> }. Batched by contract: one call per owner population per page. Labels are keyed `TYPE:id` because two populations can share a uuid. With no contributor for a population the label is `TYPE · <short id>`, honest rather than broken. A provider that throws is logged and costs names, never the list. Kept separate from `document:requirement_source` because a label is needed on every read and a compliance profile almost never. hr_document contributes EMPLOYEE.

Turns an (ownerType, ownerId) pair into the free-form facet profile that requirement matching runs against, plus the anchor date a due-by is counted from and the end date a SUBJECT_END retention basis counts from. Default export: { ownerType, getProfile(tenantId, ownerId), getProfiles?(tenantId, ownerIds) }. This is why `document` can express 'a FOREIGN full-time employee must hold a valid work permit within 30 days of hire' without ever importing `hr` — the requirement stores opaque facets and a contributor supplies the vocabulary. Implement `getProfiles` unless the population is tiny: without it a 500-owner compliance matrix becomes 500 round trips. A provider that throws is logged and skipped; its facets go missing, which surfaces as an unmatched requirement rather than a 500.
Custom per-file action surfaced in the context menu (e.g. OCR, convert-to-PDF, export).
Lifecycle hooks for upload/delete/move events (thumbnails, indexing, antivirus, …).
Custom previewer/renderer for specific MIME types or groups (e.g. office, CAD, 3D, markdown).
External storage backend mounted as a virtual Drive folder (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive).

Satellite modules contribute custom block types (client BlockDefinition, default export) to the page builder. Resolved into the client block map modules/common/ui/generated/module-blocks.ts and merged by BlockRegistry.ts — never the server extension map. Contract: docs/marketplace-block-seam.md.

Server source (default export implementing CollectionSource) that feeds a collection binding's items live instead of from CMS rows, so a bound template page SSRs one URL per item without duplicating data. A binding selects a source by its contribution `key` (sourceKey). See server/dynamic_page.collection-source.ts.

Where the page editor's review comments are kept (threads on blocks, replies, resolving). Default export: PageReviewCommentStore { list, create, get, remove }, each called with the subject type and source. The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none the editor shows no Comments tab and the comments API answers 409. Contributed by `comments`; dynamic_page does not import it.

The visitor-facing strings of a module's public blocks (04-commerce 11 item 6.1). The public site's only I18nProvider is SiteChrome's; it carries dynamic_page's visitor keys plus every contribution active for the tenant. Default export: VisitorMessagesContribution { prefixes: string[] (each '<own moduleId>.' or narrower, ending with '.'), dictionaries: { locale: messages } }; only keys under the prefixes are sent, with the texts stored in `translation` laid over them. A disabled module contributes nothing; a contribution that fails to load or breaks the contract is skipped (its keys stay English). See server/dynamic_page.visitor-messages.ts.

An external B2B data provider (company search, people search, company/person enrichment). Satellite modules like enrichment_clay contribute their implementation here. Contributions carry no requires edge: the satellite pulls the contract with `import type` and names this point only in its manifest.
A national e-signature / eID backend. Sandboxed community plugins (the esign plugin family, e.g. @smartid/esign) contribute their implementation here.

Runtime-discovered contribution sources (e.g. sandboxed community plugins). A contributor default-exports a source fn (tenantId, point) => ExternalContribution[]; hosts read it via listExternalContributions().

Where experiment exposures and conversions are recorded and counted. Default export: { track(tenantId, { name, anonymousId, properties }), countByProperty(tenantId, { name, propertyKey, matchProps }), timeseries(tenantId, { name, matchProps, from, to, interval }) } (the type is ExperimentEventSink in server/experiment.events.ts). The first contribution by order is used; with none, exposures are not recorded and results show zeros.

How many of each deployment-wide counted thing exist now (fleet step 3b.11, owner rule S11 rule 7), shown in the console next to the license cap. Default export: DeploymentUsageProvider () => Promise<Record<string, number>>; the module that owns the rows answers its own keys (tenant: tenants; fleet on a control plane: nodes, regions) and {} when it counts nothing here. Display only: enforcement recounts under its own lock and never reads this. A contributor that throws or times out leaves its keys unknown (null), never a 500.

A deployment-wide CAP on what the entitlement sources grant (fleet step 3b.10, decision F23, owner rule S11): the stricter of a tenant's plan and the deployment's license. Default export: EntitlementCeilingProvider { ceiling() => Promise<EntitlementFeature[] | null>, baseline() => EntitlementFeature[] | null }. Applied after the additive merge of entitlement_source as a minimum: a BOOLEAN is on only when both say on, a LIMIT is the smaller (-1 loses to any finite value); it also caps the ungated and wildcard answers, since a cap is global. A key no contributor names is untouched, and with no contributor (or every one answering null) nothing changes. Never a grant: on a key the plan never declared it can only add a refusal. A separate point because entitlement_source is additive by contract, so a cap contributed there would widen. Asked in a system context and memoised per process for 10 s, 1 s when a contributor answered its baseline (invalidateEntitlementCeiling drops it); the per-tenant cache stays the plan's answer. A contributor whose ceiling() throws or hangs answers its own baseline() (the un-licensed baseline, S11 rule 5), never deny-all; one that cannot be loaded, or whose baseline() throws, fails the check closed (500).

Told that a tenant's entitlements just changed. Default export: EntitlementChangeListener { entitlementChanged(tenantId) => Promise<void> }. Announced by invalidateFeatureCache, which every write that changes what a tenant is entitled to already calls after it commits (a plan assigned, cancelled or lapsed, a grace period started or ended, a catalogue entitlement granted, revoked or expired), so a module that keeps state derived from an entitlement (tenant_domain suspends the custom domains a plan no longer includes) reacts at once instead of on its next sweep. Detached: the announcing write does not wait, and a listener that fails is logged and counted, never surfaced to that write; a listener must be idempotent and keep its own periodic reconcile as the safety net. Platform gate: the reaction is the platform's, not a tenant feature, so a listener runs whatever the tenant switched on. A catalogue edit that changes many tenants at once (a plan's features) is not announced per tenant; it reaches listeners through the cache TTL and their sweeps.

Where a tenant's entitlements come from. Default export: (tenantId) => Promise<EntitlementState | null>, where EntitlementState is { status, gracePeriodEndsAt, features[] } and null means 'this source has no arrangement for that tenant' — meaningfully different from a state whose status is not live. Declared so the gate never imports a subscription rail: before it, fifteen modules had to require tenant_subscription just to ask 'may this tenant send mail', which is also why five unexpected mutual-import pairs existed (DUP-01 step 5). Sources are ADDITIVE: a tenant holding both a subscription and a granted bundle gets the union, so a second source can be added without re-deciding precedence per key. With ZERO sources registered the gate allows everything — that is the standalone-installability contract, not a loophole. A source that THROWS fails the check closed (500), because 'cannot answer' is not 'absent'.

Sellable pieces inside a module (ADR-0015): a module that sells or switches on part of itself piece by piece declares each piece here, one contribution per piece under its own module id, without editing feature_gate. The contribution key is the piece id (a lower-case letter, then letters and digits, no underscore, at most 24) and the static metadata is { label, description? } in English; the export is the module's <module>.piece-list file, the readable twin of these contributions (definePieces of feature_gate.pieces.ts), which the module's test pins to module.json. The keys are derived, never written: the entitlement key bundle:<moduleId>_<pieceId> (what a licence names, a catalogue product grants and the gate checks) and the catalogue product bundle_<moduleId>_<pieceId> (one feature-only, one-time add-on per piece). Read by feature_gate.pieces.registry.ts (metadata only, a system context, every contribution checked against the point's zod schema and key patterns; a malformed one is dropped with a warning) for the shared piece check feature_gate.piece-check.ts (pieceStates(tenantId, moduleId): the licence ceiling first, then ROOT, monetization off, checkFeatureAccess; any failure is a 503), and by the vendor's licence tool from the module.json files. A piece is a key, never a module: the module's code ships whole and the key decides who may add the piece's content.

Paid client content served behind a ticket instead of as a public chunk (dashboard phase 33, ADR-0016). A module declares one contribution per pack, keyed by the pack id: entry (module-relative source of the value, ui/ or server/), symbol (its named export or default), gate (module-relative source of gate(value, licensed), which swaps the value for grey 'Unlicensed' stand-ins when the licence check fails), host (the module specifiers a pack reads from the page's registry globalThis.__KUI_PACK_HOST__ instead of bundling; a closed list, any other import outside the module fails the build), bundle (optional: package specifiers bundled into the pack together with what they import, the closed exception for a pack written against an engine API such as @kuraykaraaslan/kui-viewer/designer-kit), integerStep and decimalShift (how the per-download mark moves the pack's numbers, feature_gate.pack-mark.ts). scripts/build-protected-packs.mts bundles every declared pack into .protected-packs/ before next build (development builds on demand). The owning module issues tickets from its own route through issuePackTicket (feature_gate.protected-packs.ts: an audit row per ticket, strict); GET /api/feature_gate/packs/[moduleId]/[packId]?t= serves the marked pack to a valid ticket only. The export is the module's server file listing its packs, the readable twin of these contributions, which the module's test pins to module.json.

Runs in the NODE APP: the region's aggregate billing block for the agent's heartbeat (Decision 20, F25), class G. Default export: () => Promise<BillingAggregate> (fleet_protocol plan-catalog.ts: windowDays and rows of integers per plan code and currency, no tenant ids; products the fleet did not publish under 'unmanaged'). The first answer valid under the schema is used; a provider that throws adds nothing. fleet_agent imports none of its providers.

Runs in the NODE APP: takes the license leases of a heartbeat acknowledgement (HeartbeatAck.licenseLeases, carried by fleet from fleet:heartbeat_leases) for the deployment's license client (13-fleet-license.md step 3b.5). Default export: (leases: unknown[]) => Promise<{ accepted: boolean; reason?: string }>; the contribution verifies every lease itself (the agent and the loopback pass them unread). Every contribution receives the leases and the first answer is returned to the agent; none means the node runs without a license module (503 to the agent). fleet_agent imports none of its providers.

Runs in the NODE APP: the deployment license's health as G metrics for the agent's heartbeat (13-fleet-license.md step 3b.5). Default export: () => Promise<Record<string, number>>; only the closed set LICENSE_METRIC_NAMES (fleet_protocol telemetry.classes) survives, as safe integers from -1. A provider that throws adds nothing; every contribution is merged, the first value of a name wins. fleet_agent imports none of its providers.

Runs in the NODE APP: imports the plan catalogue the control plane published for this node (Decision 20, F25), after the app verified the signed PLAN_CATALOG against its own trust bundle. Default export: (catalog: PlanCatalogBundleContent) => Promise<{ outcome: 'IMPORTED' | 'CURRENT'; version: number; products: number; prices: number }>; a version at or below the one it holds changes nothing and answers { outcome: 'CURRENT' } with the held version (it never throws for that; it throws only when it cannot write, and the agent then offers the catalogue again on the next beat); the agent also re-offers an accepted version periodically, so CURRENT is the normal answer to a re-offer. The rows stay read-only (managedBy 'fleet'). The first answer is returned to the agent; none means the node has no billing module (503 to the agent). fleet_agent imports none of its providers.

Runs in the NODE APP: every tenant's subscription snapshot for the subscription echo (fleet phase 6d.2, an internal planning document F48), class G.
