Default export: () => Promise<{ tenantId; snapshot }[]> (fleet_protocol subscription-echo.ts: product keys from the fleet catalogue, 'unmanaged' for local ones, an enum status and billing mode, a period end, seats, coupon codes, a currency; never an amount, payment or name). fleet_agent reports a tenant whose snapshot changed as a SUBSCRIPTION_CHANGED receipt; a snapshot outside the schema is skipped. The first array answered is used; a provider that throws adds nothing. fleet_agent imports none of its providers.

The license update window of fleet nodes (an internal planning document, step 3b.7). A contribution default-exports (i: { nodeIds: string[]; releasePublishedAt: Date; now: Date }) => Promise<string[]>: the node ids, out of those asked, whose licenses stopped covering platform updates before the release was published; a node it does not name is admitted. A direct deployment to a refused node is refused (REJECTED_UPDATES_ENDED) and a rollout plan skips it. Fail closed: a provider that throws, times out, is paused or answers anything but distinct asked ids makes the read fail, and nothing is sent to the nodes in question (a direct deployment answers 503, a plan does not start, a running plan creates no deployment that step). No contribution admits every node. fleet_release imports none of its providers.

Alert conditions another module owns, reconciled by fleet's level-triggered alert sweep like its own (one alert per node and kind). The contribution declares the kinds it owns with their notification titles in metadata.kinds ({ "<area>.<what>": "<title>" }); a kind fleet evaluates itself, or one an earlier contribution declared, is not its own. It default-exports (ds: DataSource, now: Date) => Promise<{ nodeId, kind, severity: 'medium' | 'high' | 'critical', detail: Record<string, string | number | boolean> }[]>: the conditions that hold now, codes and numbers only. The answer is validated strictly and void as a whole on any undeclared kind or malformed entry; a provider that throws or answers something void is held: its open alerts are neither updated nor resolved that tick. fleet imports none of its providers.

Invoked after a command's state or progress was committed by the node's ack, a progress event or its result. Default export: (evt: { commandId, nodeId, kind, status, phase, percent, resultCode }) => Promise<void>; metadata only (never the envelope or a result body), the row as the database holds it when the hook runs (writes that land close together may be reported with the same, newest state: the hook is a trigger, the command rows are the truth). Each contribution runs in its own try/catch and a failing hook never fails the agent request; delivery is best effort and at most once per write, so a consumer reconciles from the command rows too. The edge points consumer to fleet; fleet imports none of its listeners.

Signed leases another module mints for a node, carried to it in the heartbeat acknowledgement (HeartbeatAck.licenseLeases; an internal planning document, step 3b.4). A contribution default-exports (nodeId: string, nowSeconds: number) => Promise<unknown[]>: the documents to hand to that node now, which fleet carries without reading. Every answer is bounded (at most 16 documents and 32 KiB per node, plain JSON objects); a provider that throws or answers something else contributes nothing that heartbeat, because a lease is renewed with slack and the next heartbeat asks again. fleet imports none of its providers.

The tenantStatusDelta of a heartbeat acknowledgement (an internal planning document section 8.3, decision F1): what the tenant directory changed since the cursor the node reported about tenants that live, or lived until the change, on that node. A contribution default-exports (nodeId: string, cursor: number, nowSeconds: number) => Promise<{ entries: { tenantId, status, assignmentVersion, homeNodeId }[], cursor: number } | null>: one entry per tenant (at most 256), the directory's effective status (never UNAVAILABLE), the assignment version and the home node at that version, and the cursor to report next. The answer is checked against the wire contract (fleet_protocol tenant-status-delta) and void as a whole otherwise; a provider that throws or answers something void contributes nothing that heartbeat and no cursor is sent, so the node asks again from the same position. The first answer wins; fleet imports none of its providers.

The Fleet ID client of one node on its console page (an internal planning document, FID-06, decision F29): what the node reported for it, what is registered, and the two actions, register the report and revoke. A contribution default-exports { status(nodeId), register({ nodeId, reportHash, actorId }), revoke({ nodeId, actorId }) }; fleet checks the node and its region scope and the operator's rights, the contribution reads the node's report and writes the client. The contribution's metadata MUST name the permissions its data needs: metadata.permissions = { read, register, revoke }; the routes require them on top of fleet.nodes.read / fleet.nodes.manage, and a contribution without them is ignored (fail closed). The status is checked against fleet's contract (fleet.node-identity-client.port.ts) and refusals are thrown as the contributor's own errors with a details.reason. The first contribution answers; fleet imports none of its providers.

The licenses of one node on its console page (an internal planning document, step 3b.6): list them, list the ones it could take, assign and unassign. A contribution default-exports { list(nodeId), options(nodeId), assign({ nodeId, nodePublicKey, licenseId, actorId }), unassign({ nodeId, licenseId, actorId }) }; fleet checks the node, its region scope and its lifecycle, and hands over the signing key the node enrolled with (raw Ed25519, base64url), so no key is ever typed. The contribution's metadata MUST name the permissions its data needs: metadata.permissions = { read, options, assign, unassign }; the routes require them on top of fleet.nodes.read / fleet.nodes.manage, and a contribution without them is ignored (fail closed). Rows are checked against fleet's contract (fleet.node-licenses.port.ts) and refusals are thrown as the contributor's own errors. The first contribution answers; fleet imports none of its providers.

The release signing keys a trust bundle carries (ciKeys, releaseManagerKeys). A contribution default-exports (now: Date) => Promise<{ ciKeys: ReleaseKeySlot[]; releaseManagerKeys: ReleaseKeySlot[] }> and answers ONLY the keys usable at `now` (not revoked, not expired, past their cooling-off), each as { kid, publicKey, notAfter }. The publish path merges every contribution, validates the answer strictly and fails closed (503) when a provider throws or answers something else; no contribution means no release keys. fleet imports none of its providers.

Whether the Fleet ID hub holds a published, intact transfer notice for a region's identityNoticeRef (an internal planning document, F45/F46), for the compliance check zone.notice_present. Default export: { published(noticeRef: string): Promise<boolean> }. The first contribution answers; none = the notice cannot be verified and the check reports ERROR. Exists so fleet never imports the identity module: auth_oidc_provider answers it with the text its consent screen would show.

Modules act on a submitted form — crm_lead turns one into a lead, support could turn one into a ticket. FAILS OPEN: the submission row is stored before any sink runs, so a throwing sink costs one unprocessed record whose data is still on disk, and can never fail the visitor's request.

`(tenantId, { employeeIds, from, to }) => Promise<WorkEntryInput[]>` (types in `hr_attendance/server/hr_attendance.work-entry.types`, import them with `import type`). Each contribution reports facts for the range; its `key` becomes the rows' `sourceModuleId`, whatever the provider claims. Generation diffs per source, so a contributor is the owner of its rows: an entry it stops reporting is removed, unless locked. FAIL-SAFE: a contributor that throws keeps its existing rows untouched (left out of the diff), so a broken module cannot empty a month of leave days. hr_leave contributes taken leave days and hr_timesheet the per-day breakdown frozen at approval; neither requires hr_attendance.

A source of work figures for an employee set over a run's period (hr_attendance today; hr_timesheet, hr_expense, hr_loan later). Default export `PayrollInputSource` from `hr_payroll/server/payroll.input-sources` (import type): `collect({ tenantId, employeeIds, periodKey, periodStart, periodEnd }) → { work?: Record<employeeId, Partial<WorkSummary>> }`, and optionally `lock({ …, runId })`, called after a run is processed or paid so the source freezes what payroll counted. Metadata: `{ label, overrides: Array<keyof WorkSummary> }` — a listed field REPLACES earlier figures, every other field ADDS. A throwing source is dropped and reported in `failedSources` (never shown as zero hours). Payroll requires none of its contributors.

A named calculator a CODE_PROVIDER salary rule calls by providerKey (a country pack's tax or social-security maths). Default export `SalaryRuleProvider` from `hr_payroll/server/payroll.rule-providers` (import type): `compute({ rule, lines, context, params, tenantId?, baseMinor?, ytd? }) -> { amountMinor, baseMinor?, rate?, quantity?, skip?, extraLines?, ytd?, preview? }`, optionally `validate(rule) -> string[]` and `notice({ tenantId }) -> { code, message } | null`. `baseMinor` is the rule's baseSelector resolved at that point of the walk. A `preview` marks the lines and the result: the payroll pages show the provider's notice and approve/pay refuse the figures with 409 PREVIEW_ONLY. Metadata: `{ label, countryCode? }`. A tenant without the contributor gets a per-line PROVIDER_NOT_INSTALLED error from the rule test, never a crashed run.

Asked before a job position, grade or employment type is deleted whether the contributing module still holds rows pointing at it. Default export: (tenantId, { kind, id }) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the module. hr counts its OWN rows directly (employees; for a grade also the job positions planned at it), so a contribution is only needed for satellites: hr_contract counts the employment terms that carry a position, grade or employment type (hr_payroll has no catalog columns). Data gate: a contributor is asked while its module is switched off for the tenant, because its rows still point at the catalog (EXT-1). hr_document holds no reference (a requirement facet on an employment type only stops matching) and neither does hr_recruitment (its employment type is a fixed enum, not a catalog uuid). Kinds: POSITION | GRADE | EMPLOYMENT_TYPE. The sites/cost-centers half of the old hr_org point now lives in organization:reference_check.

Invoked after every committed lifecycle write. Default export: (tenantId, evt: { employeeId, movementType, effectiveAt, previous, next }) => Promise<void>. Each contribution is awaited inside its OWN try/catch, so a broken satellite can never fail a hire. hr_onboarding spawns a checklist on HIRE, hr_asset raises return tasks on TERMINATE, hr_payroll stops recurring pay.

Chips on the employee detail header, served by GET /api/hr/employees/[employeeId]/summary-chips (hr.employees.read, like the detail read). Default export: (tenantId, employeeId) => Promise<Array<{ key, label, value, vars?, permission? }>>. `key` is a dictionary key prefix of the contributing module: the header renders t(`${key}.label`, label, vars) and t(`${key}.value`, value, vars), so `label` and `value` are the English text and `vars` fill the translation's {{placeholders}}. A chip with `permission` is dropped for a viewer who lacks it. hr_leave shows the remaining annual leave, hr_contract the running contract, hr_asset the assets held. Behaviour gate: a chip disappears with its module. A failing contribution is skipped — a missing chip is cosmetic, a 500 is not.

A satellite adds a tab to the employee detail page. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'hr.employee.tabs': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'hr.employee.tabs', component, order, props: { slotTabId, slotTabLabel } } and the page resolves it through the generated client component map, never the server extension map. Props received: { tenantId, employeeId }.

Overlays an employment status that a sibling module owns (ONLEAVE from hr_leave; later SUSPENDED/SECONDED) onto hr's movement-ledger projection. Default export: (tenantId, { employeeIds, at }) => Promise<Array<{ employeeId, status }>>. Declared so hr never imports a satellite — hr is the base of the HR dependency graph and every hr_* module requires it.

A regional/country e-invoicing adapter (UBL-TR/GİB, Peppol BIS, FatturaPA, Chorus Pro, ZUGFeRD, CFDI, GST IRP, US Stripe Tax). Adapters come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @earsiv/invoice, @peppol/invoice); the host's adapters/registry resolves them per tenant through listExternalContributions. Routing (region vs issuer-country) is carried in each contribution's metadata { kind, code }. Shared XML helpers (xml.util, cii_xml) and the InvoiceAdapter contract stay in the host. One accepted in-module path (2026-10-17): with earsivIntegrator = gib_direct a TR invoice is submitted by the host's own GİB portal client (adapters/tr_gib_direct.*), with or without a TR plugin, because it runs on the tenant's GİB portal session and SMS-OTP signing, which a sandbox cannot hold; every other integrator goes through the plugin.

A header button of an asset's drawer on the Sites & assets page that another module adds, a button that opens its own drawer (never a tab): the Scene setup (dashboard_viewer, the drawing the asset shows and which of its devices feeds which part of it). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_asset.asset.actions': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_asset.asset.actions', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, assetId } (plus its manifest props) and draws its button and its drawer. The drawer's header shows every contribution beside its own actions, ordered by the contribution's order, only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set), each isolated in an error boundary. iot_asset imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

Asked before an IoT asset node is deleted whether the contributing module still holds live rows pointing at it (an iot_twin site model, an iot_alarm rule scoped to the node). Default export: (tenantId, iotAssetId) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the module; a contributor that cannot answer blocks the delete (EXT-3). The node's own relations are not references: they are deleted with it.

Evaluates a device profile's alarm rules for the action.alarm_rules node of the iot host (OD-88, OD-154). The node is this module's, so a tenant whose alarm module is switched off still deploys and runs its root flow and stores its data; the node asks the tenant's active contributor (iot_alarm) and passes the message on unchanged when there is none. Default export: IotAlarmEvaluator { evaluate(input) => Promise<IotAlarmTransitionOut[]>, isOutage?(error) }; the node sends each transition on its created / updated / cleared port. One contributor (iot_alarm).

A node type that hears one device's messages outside the roots (iot-rules 01 §1.2, RL-E9). Default export: DeviceListenerContribution { nodeType, listen(params) => { devices, types } | null }; listen is pure and reads the node's own params only. When a tenant's flows load, the iot dispatch indexes every enabled node of the type by the devices it names: a device message then also reaches the listeners of its device that name its type, and a listener naming telemetry_saved makes its devices watched, so action.save_telemetry announces their stored records as telemetry_saved entries (after the commit, cause carried). Roots never change. Each contribution lists its node type in metadata.ids, and two contributions listing one type fail the registry snapshot.

Who still reads some telemetry keys of a profile, and the rewrite of those reads onto new key names (dashboard phase 39 UX-11). Default export: { renamePermission, usage(tenantId, profileId, keys) => Promise<{ moduleId, label, count, keys } | null>, rename(tenantId, profileId, { old: new }, actorUserId) => Promise<same | null> }. The profile editor asks after a save that removed keys (GET /api/iot/device-profiles/[profileId]/key-usage) and, for keys renamed in place, offers the rewrite (POST, the profile write permission and the contributor's renamePermission). iot_alarm answers with its alarm rules. A contributor that throws is reported as unverifiable, never as unused. Declared here so the profile never imports a module that reads its keys (EXT-14).

A header button of the device profile page that another module adds, a button that opens its own drawer (never a tab): the Scene setup of the profile's devices (dashboard_viewer, "bind every device of this profile that has no scene to one drawing", which writes each device's own binding and never a profile default). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device_profile.profile.actions': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device_profile.profile.actions', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, profileId } and draws its button and its drawer. The page puts every contribution among the header's actions, ordered by the contribution's order, only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set), each isolated in an error boundary. iot_device_profile imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

Which provisioning strategies an active module answers devices for (docs/concepts/iot-device-profile 02 §2.1, D203). Default export: { strategies(tenantId) => Promise<ProvisionStrategy[]> } (never DISABLED). iot_provisioning answers ALLOW_CREATE_NEW_DEVICES, CHECK_PRE_PROVISIONED_DEVICES and ROLTEK_FACTORY, the strategies its v1/provision/req serves. The provisioning read (GET /api/iot/device-profiles/[profileId]/provisioning) offers DISABLED plus the served strategies the profile may take (availableStrategies), so the editor never offers a strategy no module answers; with the module off only DISABLED is offered. A display, not a gate: the PUT keeps its own rules. Declared here so the profile never imports iot_provisioning (EXT-14).

Asked before a device profile is deleted whether the contributing module still holds rows pointing at it (P-3). Default export: (tenantId, profileId) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the module. iot_device answers with its device count; iot_alarm and iot_ota will answer with their rules and assignments. Data gate: a contributor is asked while its module is off for the tenant, because its rows still point at the profile (EXT-1). Fails closed: a contributor that cannot answer blocks the delete (EXT-3). Also asked by GET /api/iot/device-profiles/usage (the profile list's device count and the delete hint; counts only). Declared here so the profile, the root of the IoT dependency chain, never imports a module that uses it.

A tab of the device profile page (iot-device-profile 03 §3.1, P-3) that another IoT module adds: Alarm rules (iot_alarm), Commands (iot_rpc), Firmware (iot_ota), Flows (iot_automation). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device_profile.profile.tabs': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device_profile.profile.tabs', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { tabId, label, labelKey, transports?, profileKeys? } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, profileId }. The page orders the tabs by the contribution order after its own, shows a tab only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set) and only when it applies to this profile, and isolates each in an error boundary; a contributed tab saves through its own module's routes. Profile scope (D206): the same generic transports / profileKeys props as the device page's tabs (iot_device_profile/ui/iot-tab-scope), matched against this profile's own transportType and builtinKey as the editor reads and saves it; neither field = every profile. tabId must not be one of the page's own (general, transport, online, limits, telemetry, config, provisioning). iot_device_profile imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

Which transport values a profile may take besides the built-in ones (OD-177, iot-gateway phase 13.3; iot-device-profile 03 D435, D436). A profile's transportType is MQTT, HTTP, ANY or a value contributed here: the lower-case id of a protocol registered at iot_gateway:protocol (isapi, snmp, rtsp) - a POLLED transport - or an upper-case NON-POLLED transport another module serves (iot_lorawan: LORAWAN for end devices, LORAWAN_GATEWAY for gateways). Whether a value is polled is its case alone. The profile, the root of the IoT chain, cannot import its contributors to ask, so each contributes one resolver: default export { describe(tenantId, id) => { id, label, labelKey?, polled, deviceCredentials? } | null, list(tenantId) => [...], parseSettings? }. deviceCredentials says whether the devices log in to the platform themselves (absent = no; a polled protocol never does): the device page hides its Credentials tab and iot_device issues no credential when it is false. Asked when a transport is set (create, or an update that changes it), never on a read: a profile whose contributing module was switched off or uninstalled keeps its value. Behaviour-gated: a contributor whose module is off for the tenant is not asked, so the Transport select offers only the transports of modules that are on. The first contribution that answers wins. Declared here so the profile never imports a contributor (EXT-14).

Another way to add a device, offered in the Devices page's New device drawer before "Other device" (iot_device's own create form): claiming a Roltek device with the code on its Cloud page (iot_provisioning), a camera or recorder (iot_camera), a LoRaWAN gateway or end device (iot_lorawan); the choices follow their order. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device.devices.add': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device.devices.add', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { choiceId, label, labelKey, description, descriptionKey, transports? } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, onAdded }, drawn inside the drawer, and calls onAdded after it added a device (the list re-reads). The page offers a choice only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions, and isolates it in an error boundary. `transports` (optional, iot-device 05 D292) lists the profile transports or iot_gateway protocol ids the choice adds devices of (iot_camera's isapi and rtsp): the page ignores it; a choice that offers protocols generically (iot_gateway's "Network device") reads the other choices' lists from the same slot and leaves those protocols to them, so each protocol has one way in without either naming the other. iot_device imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

A header button of the device page that another module adds, a button that opens its own drawer (the pattern of the Devices page's "Awaiting approval (n)"; never a tab): the Scene setup (dashboard_viewer, the drawing the device shows and which element feeds which part of it). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device.device.actions': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device.device.actions', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, deviceId } (plus its manifest props) and draws its button and its drawer. The page puts every contribution among the header's actions, ordered by the contribution's order, only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set), each isolated in an error boundary. iot_device imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

A header action of the Devices list that another module adds (iot-device 05 D291; owner 2026-11-04: a module's own page folds into Devices): an entry of the list's "⋯" menu that opens the contribution's own drawer, never a page, a tab or a menu item (iot_lorawan's "Gateway map" and "LoRaWAN frames", iot_lorawan_codecs' "LoRaWAN codecs"). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device.devices.actions': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device.devices.actions', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { actionId, label, labelKey } }; the menu shows one entry per contribution after the page's own entries (past a separator), in the contributions' order, with the translated label, only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions. Choosing it mounts the component with { tenantId, open: true, onClose } (plus its manifest props) inside the slot's error boundary and Suspense; the component draws its drawer and calls onClose when it closes (the host then unmounts it, so nothing of it runs while it is closed). A broken contribution is caught by the boundary and the list stays. iot_device imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

The approval view of the quarantined devices, opened from the Devices page's "Awaiting approval (n)" button in a drawer (iot_provisioning's list with Activate). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device.devices.quarantine': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device.devices.quarantine', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, onChanged } and calls onChanged after it activated devices (the list and the count re-read). The page uses the first contribution the viewer may see; without one there is no button and the list keeps its "Quarantined (n)" quick filter. iot_device imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

Asked before a device is deleted whether the contributing module still holds live rows pointing at it (D7). Default export: (tenantId, deviceId) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the module (an iot_asset relation, an open OTA campaign). Telemetry and attribute history are not references. Data gate: a contributor is asked while its module is off for the tenant (EXT-1). Fails closed: a contributor that cannot answer blocks the delete (EXT-3). Zero contributors in P1: iot_asset and iot_ota contribute in their phases.

A tab of the device page (iot-device 05 §5.3) that another IoT module adds: Alarms (iot_alarm), RPC (iot_rpc), OTA, Placement; iot_device's own Feeds (the device's reading bindings, with iot_device.bindings.read) comes the same way. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'iot_device.device.tabs': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'iot_device.device.tabs', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { tabId, label, labelKey, transports?, profileKeys? } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, deviceId }. The page orders the tabs by the contribution order, shows a tab only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions (the shell's granted set) and only when it applies to the device's profile, and isolates each in an error boundary. Profile scope (D217, iot_device_profile/ui/iot-tab-scope): transports = the profile transportType values the tab applies to (MQTT, HTTP, ANY, LORAWAN, or a protocol id registered at iot_gateway:protocol such as isapi or rtsp, compared without case; POLLED = every registered protocol); profileKeys = built-in profiles (builtinKey) it is made for whatever their transport, and naming one claims it, so a tab scoped by transports alone skips a claimed profile (only the profile's owner names it). Neither field = every device; a device without a profile shows only the unscoped tabs; the page's own tabs always show. The page learns the profile's transport and built-in key from its device read (profileTransport, profileBuiltinKey). tabId must not be one of the page's own (overview, attributes, credentials, log, and connections, the Log tab's former id). iot_device imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

A protocol the platform polls (docs/concepts/iot-gateway/phases/13, OD-175, OD-179): a module that speaks to a box that cannot push (a camera, an NVR, an SNMP agent, a vendor gateway) contributes one protocol object and contains only protocol logic; iot_gateway owns the endpoints (write-only secrets), the public-address rule, the iot-poller sidecar, the message quota and the register flow. Contribute with `key` = the protocol id (lower case, at most 32 characters, the profile's transport value) and `export` = a file whose default export is { id, label, icon, endpointSchema, addressSchema?, profileSchema?, test(endpoint, ctx), poll?(endpoint, devices, profile, ctx), discover?(endpoint, ctx), events?(endpoint, sink, ctx), streamSource?(endpoint, device, variant, ctx) } (protocol.types.ts). The host loads and validates every contribution once per process (id well formed, unique and equal to the key; schemas valid; test a function; poll, discover, events and streamSource functions when present). A protocol with `events` gets the endpoint setting `eventsEnabled` (default OFF) added by the host: a broken contribution is skipped and logged, never fatal. Catalog with code, loaded on first use (the registry) and gated per tenant by the extension runtime's contributor state for the routes; the poller, whose database login reads no module state, polls every registered protocol. `persists`: endpoints and device profiles store the protocol id, so an uninstalled module leaves references behind (a profile keeps its transport and reads 'protocol not installed'; its devices are not polled). Not external: a protocol decrypts endpoint credentials and opens connections from the platform's fixed egress addresses, which a sandboxed marketplace plugin may not do.

Who sends cert.renew (protocol 05 §5) to the device that holds a certificate (docs/concepts/iot-pki 03 §3.1, PK-09, D453). iot_pki's daily job decides when (at most 21 days left, no CSR yet, once per certificate: the ledger's renewRequestedAt) and asks the first contribution enabled for the certificate's subject tenant; the contribution decides how: which device holds the certificate, whether it is online and announced the method (hello capabilities rpc + csr, FZ-29), and the RPC itself. Default export: CertRenewTrigger { trigger({ tenantId, certificateId, deviceSerial, fingerprintSha256, actor, idempotencyKey }) => Promise<{ sent: true, deviceId, rpcId } | { sent: false, reason: 'no_device' | 'offline' | 'not_announced' | 'not_supported' | 'refused', deviceId?, detail? }> }. With none (the tenant has no iot_rpc), nothing is sent and the job asks again the next day. A point of iot_pki because iot_pki cannot import iot_rpc or iot_device (both import iot_pki).

RPC methods a module owns (D476): a module that sends its own methods through iot_rpc after its own safety rules, permission and audit (iot_esim's esim.*, iot_remote_access's tunnel.*) declares them here, one contribution per module, so no person, API key, board or flow can send them as raw or catalog RPC around it. Static metadata { label (English, what the refusal names), methods? (exact names), prefixes? (namespaces ending in '.') }; the export is the module's <module>.rpc-reserved file, the readable twin of the metadata that also mints the module's owner mark (rpcMethodOwner of iot_rpc.reserved.ts), which the module's test pins to module.json. Read by iot_rpc.reserved.ts in a system context (every contribution of the build, whatever a tenant switched on: D477), case-insensitively with - and _ alike. iot_rpc's create and cancel refuse a reserved method without the owning module's mark (an in-process object, never a request field) with 403 rpc_method_reserved, audited as iot_rpc.request.refused (owner, source); the device RPC route, the board command iot_rpc.call and the flow block action.rpc refuse it before the device is read; the board's command picker, the flow command list and catalog writes (400) leave it out (D479). A contribution may not reserve an empty prefix, a protocol 05 §5 registry method or namespace (sys., net., cfg., ota., cert., point.) nor what another module reserved: dropped with a warning (D481).

A topic kind of the /iot live namespace (docs/concepts/iot-telemetry/phases/04): default export { kind (= the contribution key), requiredPermission, parseParams(raw) -> params | null, authorize(ctx { tenantId, userId, permissions }, params) -> { room, join?, watch? } | null, snapshot?(ctx, params), parsePayload?(payload) } (iot_telemetry.live.topic.ts). The namespace checks the ticket's permission snapshot, then the kind's authorize on every subscribe, refuses any room that is not t:<tenantId>:iot.<kind>:<id> (or its #sub rooms), counts the subscription against the socket and tenant limits and joins. The kind's module publishes { kind, tenantId, room, payload, id?, sub? } to the Redis channel iot:rt after its change is durable. A kind whose module is not active for the tenant is unknown. Loaded lazily on the first subscribe (contributors such as iot_device are required by iot_telemetry, so the point must not be a boot-time edge).

A handler of the iot-worker system shell that reads iotsys:in:{p} (hello, csr, claim, prov, ar, raw session facts, unresolved RPC answers, OTA fw_state): { key, create(): { kinds, handle(entries, ctx) } } (stream_handler.types.ts). Bookkeeping only: a handler never writes telemetry or attributes (OD-87); a flow input it produces goes to iot:in through iot_device's stream writer. Several handlers of one kind run in contribution order; a failing one is isolated. P1 declares the registry; the shell and its handlers come with P2 (iot_device/03).
Receives a delivered message for an alias and answers where it belongs. Contributors return a target ref plus CREATE/APPEND; this module never learns what a lead or a ticket is.
An email sending backend. Backends come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @smtp/mail, @sendgrid/mail); no in-tree module provides one, and the host reads plugins only.

The MCP tools a module offers on its own MCP server (/api/mcp/<moduleId>; docs/phases/57-mcp-server D57-4). Default export: one defineMcpTool({ name, title, description, kind, permission, input, output, annotations, idempotency?, run }) or an array of them, imported from common/server/common.mcp-contracts, never from mcp_server or the MCP SDK. `permission` is a permission of the contributing module that an API key may hold (phase 48 D48-3), exactly as its own routes check it; `run` receives the verified caller (tenant, the person it acts as, the credential), validated input and an abort signal, and returns mcpOk(summary, data, foreign?) or mcpFail(code, message). The host owns authentication, the permission check, limits, audit, timeouts, the size cap, the error envelope and the fencing of foreign text. metadata: { label, ids: the tool names it exports (exactly those) }. The boot guard mcp-tools refuses the boot on a malformed tool: name ({verb}_{noun}, an approved verb, at most 48 characters), description (one sentence plus Precondition:, Output:, Errors:, at most 600 characters), annotations, schemas, idempotency for the keyed verbs, a permission that is not the contributor's or not key-grantable, a duplicate name, ids that differ from the export, and (until 57.6) any write tool. Loaded in a system context, process-wide, by the boot guard and on first use; never while a module evaluates (lazyContributors). Contributing is not depending: any module contributes from its own folder and mcp_server imports none of them.

A module that knows how to bill one OPEN metering subject kind (an organisation, a site, a project ...). Default export: { key?, subjectType, resolveBillTo(tenantId, subjectId) } where subjectType is the upper-case slug it serves and resolveBillTo returns { customerEmail, customerName, customerCountryCode, walletUserId? } or null when the subject cannot be billed. Consulted by the billing run (runBilling / billRun) for every subject type other than TENANT, USER and SUBSCRIPTION, and only when the run has something to charge. With no resolver for a type, or one that returns null, the run is marked FAILED with a clear error; it is never silently skipped. Values the caller passes explicitly win over the resolver's.

Asked before a module is installed or re-activated for a tenant, and when a billing rail reconciles after an entitlement is taken away: may this tenant have this module? Default export: (tenantId, moduleId) => Promise<{ entitled: boolean, message?: string }>. A contributor returns entitled:true for anything it has no objection to, including every module while its own gate (monetization) is off; a contributor that only caps (source 'ceiling', the platform license edition of fleet_license) is left out when deciding whether the answer is 'plan'; the first objection wins and its message reaches the user as a 403. Declared so module_lifecycle never imports tenant_subscription — the rail needs this module back to close modules on a downgrade, so the arrow can only point inward. With ZERO contributors every module is allowed (standalone installability). FAILS CLOSED: a contributor that throws is 'cannot answer', not 'entitled', and denies with a 503. Contributions are NOT filtered by the tenant's enabled modules — a tenant that switches the billing rail off must not bypass it.

A host that stores keys of other modules' contributions in its own data (an automation flow's node types, a board's widgets, a page's blocks, a setting naming a provider) answers for them here (docs/phases/37-extensions/06). Default export: ReferenceHolder { listReferences(tenantId, moduleId) => { label, count, sample? }, sweep(tenantId, moduleId) => { removed } }. listReferences feeds the impact preview before a deactivation or uninstall and the orphan report; sweep runs only when the module's data is purged, never on disable. A data-gate point: a holder answers whatever its own state.
A chat-platform backend (Telegram, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp). Sandboxed marketplace plugins contribute send, connect, startLink and handleWebhook; the host owns linking, queueing and rate limits.

Another source of the top bar's one bell (the IoT alarms), so it does not add a second bell. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'notification_inapp.bell': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'notification_inapp.bell', component, order, scope }. Props received: { tenantId, onItems(key, source), onCount(key, n) }. A source hands its items up with onItems under its own key (a NotificationSource of common's notification menu: label, items with their time, look, page and inline action, the unread count for the badge, a header action, its page; null when the viewer may not see it): they join the notifications in one list, newest first, with a filter per source (docs/phases/07-dashboard/40, D40-16). A contribution that draws a section above the list instead reports what still wants the viewer's attention through onCount and that joins the badge. Contributions stay mounted while the panel is closed (hidden), so a source keeps its items and counts live; it renders nothing when the viewer may not see it.

Read seam for a tenant's mail brand. Default export: { load(tenantId) } returning a MailBrandPatch { name, logoLight, logoDark, primaryColor, baseUrl } or null (notification_mail/server/notification_mail.brand.types#MailBrandSource). The same four-field allowlist the status page reads, plus the tenant's own verified origin for links; no HTML, CSS, footer or sender name can be contributed. Every value is validated again by notification_mail (HTTPS-only logos, hex colours, escaped names). A missing or empty source means the platform default, never an error. Merged first-non-null per field, cached 5 minutes in Redis under notification_mail:brand:<tenantId>; contributors invalidate that key from their write paths.

A delivery channel (mail, sms, push, inapp, or any open slug such as telegram). Default export: { channel, canDeliver?, deliver } implementing NotificationChannelProvider. A NEW channel (not one of the four core ids) must declare static `metadata` on its contribution so the policy can decide without loading it: { label, addressKind: 'EMAIL'|'SMS'|'ACCOUNT'|'EXTERNAL', respectsQuietHours: boolean } (respectsQuietHours is required; EXTERNAL channels resolve their own address in canDeliver and report no_address when unlinked). Its per-user toggle lives in user_preferences.channelPrefs[channel]. The dispatcher resolves policy BEFORE calling a provider, so a provider must not re-check preferences, category opt-outs or quiet hours — doing so applies the policy twice. Declared so `notification` never imports a channel module: the dispatcher stays installable with zero channels, and a tenant only gets the channels it has.

An ADDRESS-level gate: may we write to this address at all? Default export: { addressKind: 'EMAIL'|'SMS', isSuppressed(tenantId, address, { purpose }) } implementing SuppressionProvider. Separate from preferences because it answers a different question about a different subject — preferences need an account, suppression works on a guest address, a bounced mailbox or somebody who never had a login. Consulted BEFORE the CRITICAL exemption: urgency waives what the RECIPIENT chose, never what the ADDRESS is. A provider must FAIL CLOSED (an address it cannot evaluate is suppressed); the dispatcher fails OPEN on a provider error, because a broken provider knows nothing about anybody. Declared so `notification` never imports a CRM domain.

failOpen.reason: A provider that throws knows nothing about any address; refusing every message would also stop password resets and security alerts.
failOpen.when: transactional and critical purposes only; marketing and other commercial purposes fail closed (consent, EXT-3)

extensionPoints.description: The `ai` service as observability uses it: incident analysis and embeddings, the price table and usage log behind the GenAI cost views, and the one wrapper around every provider call that GenAI tracing installs. Default export: AiPeer { canComplete, chat, embed, calcCostUsd, usageLogEntity, setCallWrapper }. Contributed by `ai`; observability (Core) does not import it. With none, every ai-backed feature degrades as it does when `ai` is switched off (no analysis, no embedding, an unknown cost, no tracing wrapper).

A module reports what is wrong right now so it enters the alert pipeline (routing, grouping, silences, the dependency graph) instead of growing its own notifier. Default export: { listFiring(tenantId) } implementing AlertSourceProvider; each spec is { key, title, severity?, labels?, annotations? } and becomes an alert whose identity is `<moduleId>:<key>`. State-based: the pipeline raises what is listed and resolves what the module raised before and no longer lists. A provider that throws leaves the alerts it raised untouched (failing to look is not recovery). `entity` and `monitorId` labels are ignored: the pipeline assigns `ext:<moduleId>:<key>` as the entity so a contribution cannot claim to be another system's parent. Used by device alarms, fleet node health, automation failures and payment provider outages.

A module reports the changes it knows of (deploys, configuration, module and flag switches) so an incident can show what changed in the hour before it started. Default export: { listChanges(tenantId, from, to) } implementing ChangeEventProvider; each spec is { at, kind, title, actor?, ref? }. A provider that throws is skipped, the other sources still answer. The audit log is read as a built-in source for module, flag, setting and release actions.

Where a published post-mortem is filed as a versioned document. Default export: DocumentPort { publishVersion(tenantId, { documentId, incidentId, postmortemId, title, markdown, isPrivate, actorId, changeNote }) => { documentId, versionNo } | null }. The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, the post-mortem is published without a document (the row says so). Contributed by `document`; observability (Core) does not import it.

Where an incident's internal notes are kept (the response workflow's notes, and their removal when a resolved incident ages out). Default export: IncidentNoteSink { create(tenantId, { subjectType, subjectId, content, authorUserId?, authorName? }) => { commentId }, list(tenantId, { subjectType, subjectId }) => records, deleteForSubjects(tenantId, { subjectType, subjectIds }) }. The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, adding a note is a clear 409 ("Notes need the comments module"), listing returns nothing and retention has nothing to remove. Contributed by `comments`; observability (Core) does not import it.

Where an incident's follow-up tasks are kept. Default export: IncidentTaskSink { create(tenantId, { title, priority, assigneeUserId, dueAt, relatedType, relatedId }, actorUserId?) => { taskId }, list(tenantId, { relatedType, relatedId }) => records }. The first contribution by order that is enabled for the tenant is used; with none, adding a follow-up is a clear 409 ("Follow-up tasks need the tasks module") and listing returns nothing. Contributed by `tasks`; observability (Core) does not import it.

The `on_call` service as observability uses it: paging and resolving by dedup key for alert targets, the on-call roster for the MCP view, and the watchdog's check that the paging self-test has not gone silent. Default export: OnCallPeer { page, resolveByDedupKey, listSchedules, silentSelfTests }. Contributed by `on_call`; observability (Core) does not import it. With none, alerts are not paged, the roster is empty and the watchdog reports ok.

A module reports the external endpoints it depends on so they become uptime monitors (e.g. a configured national-id or e-signature provider). Default export: { listTargets(tenantId) } implementing ProbeTargetProvider; each target is { key, name, type, target, intervalSeconds?, timeoutMs?, expectedStatus?, degradedLatencyMs? } and becomes a monitor with sourceKey `<moduleId>:<key>`. The provider owns that monitor's identity, target and active flag: it is created on first sight, updated when the spec changes, and DEACTIVATED (never deleted) when the provider stops reporting it. A provider that throws leaves its monitors untouched; an operator opts a target out by deleting its monitor. Return [] for an unconfigured provider. Declared so provider health has ONE source (the uptime monitor) and contributing modules never import observability or grow their own health checker.

The `search` service as observability uses it: incidents are indexed on open, edit and resolve, and similar incidents are found by full text. Default export: SearchPeer { index, remove, search }. Contributed by `search`; observability (Core) does not import it. With none, nothing is indexed and similar-incident lookup uses only the other signals.

Where a tenant lives, asked by the governance layer (phase 16.6 data region, phase 16.4 legal hold). Default export: { homeOf(tenantId) => { region: string | null, legalHold: boolean } | null } implementing TenantHomeProvider; null means this contributor knows nothing about the tenant. The first contributor that answers wins. The intended contributor is fleet_directory (the routing record's home region and its legal hold), declared as a point so observability never depends on the fleet modules. A contributor that throws or times out is skipped: the answer then falls back to the workspace setting (region) or to no hold, never to a refusal of a customer's data.

A module adds a way to reach a person (voice, Slack, Teams, a pager gateway). Default export: { isAvailable?(tenantId), deliver(input) => { ok } | { ok:false, reason } } implementing OnCallChannelProvider, selected by channel id (the contribution key). push, sms and mail are not contributed here: they go through the notification dispatcher. Voice is delivered only by a contribution with key 'voice'; the keypad digit goes back to the voiceCallbackUrl it was given.

Hears the result of every self-test of the paging path, outside the paging path itself. Default export: { onSelfTest(report) } implementing OnCallHealthSink. The intended contributor is observability's heartbeat monitor. A sink that throws is logged and ignored.

Refuses an on-call seat the workspace's plan does not include. Default export: { checkSeats({ tenantId, seats, current, added }) => { ok: true } | { ok: false, message, details? } } implementing OnCallLimitGuard. A seat is a distinct person in the participant list of any layer of a live schedule; the guard is asked before a write that would raise that count (never for one that does not, so a downgraded workspace keeps editing what it has). A refusal becomes a 403 carrying the guard's details. Declared so on_call never imports a billing or governance module (observability contributes the plan limit).

failOpen.reason: A quota guard: a contributor that cannot answer (billing or cache outage) must not stop a rotation being edited; the cost is that a broken guard over-admits, which the operator's usage view makes visible (EXT-3).

extensionPoints.description: A module adds a KIND of escalation target (a team, a role, a shift lead). Default export: { resolve(tenantId, ref) => user ids, describe?(tenantId, ref) } implementing OnCallTargetProvider. A policy step names it as { type: 'extension', key, ref } where key is this contribution's key. Resolved when the step STARTS; a provider that throws leaves the step empty (noted on the page) and the policy falls through. Policies store the key, so removing the contributor leaves references behind (validation reports them).

Told after a paid channel (sms, voice) accepted a page, with { tenantId, pageId, userId, channel, outcome: 'ok', idempotencyKey, at }. Default export: { onDelivered(event) } implementing OnCallUsageSink. Best-effort: a sink that throws is logged and ignored and a delivery is never delayed or failed by it; the idempotency key is deterministic across a retry of the same step. The intended contributor is observability's metering of SMS and voice pages.

Answers whether a GL account of the tenant's ledger exists and is active, for a cost center's glAccountId (organization.06). Default export: (tenantId, accountId) => Promise<{ isActive: boolean } | null>; null = no such account. With no contributor (accounting not installed or switched off) there is no ledger to point at and a glAccountId is refused. Fails closed: a contributor that throws refuses the write. Declared so organization (Core) never imports accounting (Pro): the higher edition contributes, as the edition guard requires.

Asked before a legal entity, site or cost center is retired whether the contributing module still holds rows pointing at it. Default export: (tenantId, { kind, id }) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the module. Declared so organization never imports hr (or accounting, inventory, procurement…) — organization is the BASE of the ERP graph and every consumer requires it, so the arrow can only point inward. Kinds: LEGAL_ENTITY | SITE | COST_CENTER.

A gateway-specific coupon-checkout adapter. The coupon module validates a LOCAL code + computes the discount server-side, then asks the matching gateway adapter to turn it into checkout params (a one-off Stripe coupon, an iyzico negative basket line, a PayPal discount line). Nothing is synced to the gateway's coupon registry; the local code is the single source of truth. Payment gateway satellites contribute their adapter here.

A payment gateway implementation (Stripe, PayPal, Iyzico, ...). Contributed by sandboxed community plugins under marketplace (the `@<vendor>/pay` family, e.g. @stripe/pay); the host discovers them via the extension registry. No gateway ships in-tree. Inbound webhooks are the deliberate exception (decided 2026-10-17): Stripe and PayPal signature checks and the iyzico callback re-verification stay in the host (payment.webhook.*), because the host verifies the vendor's word with secrets it holds and a sandboxed plugin's claim that a payment succeeded must not move money; plugins never receive or judge inbound webhooks.

Told after a subscription plan is created, updated, deleted or has a feature changed, so a rail can drop whatever it cached about it. Default export: (tenantId, planId?) => Promise<void>; planId omitted means 'drop this tenant's plan caches wholesale'. Sibling of payment:plan_usage and declared for the same reason — payment owns subscription_plans but two consoles write it, and only payment_subscription caches, so an edit made from tenant_subscription used to leave the other console serving the old price until its TTL expired (DUP-01). Unlike plan_usage this fails OPEN: it runs AFTER the write commits, so refusing cannot un-write the plan, only turn a successful edit into a 500. A failing invalidator is logged loudly and the write stands; staleness is TTL-bounded.

Asked before a subscription plan is deleted whether the contributing subscription rail still holds live subscriptions on it. Default export: (tenantId, planId) => Promise<{ moduleId, count, label } | null>; a non-zero count turns the delete into a 409 naming the rail. Declared so payment (which owns subscription_plans) never imports payment_subscription or tenant_subscription — both require payment, so the arrow can only point inward. Unlike organization:reference_check this point FAILS CLOSED: a rail that cannot answer blocks the delete, because orphaning live paid subscriptions is worse than an undeletable plan.

Offered to every rail that SELLS through payment when a gateway reports something about one of its charges (payment.completed / subscription.renewed|cancelled|past_due). Named for subscriptions because the two subscription rails were its first contributors, but payment.completed is offered for every payment whoever sold it — marketplace contributes here for one-off plugin sales and ignores the subscription.* actions. Default export: (event: SubscriptionRailEvent) => Promise<void>; a rail matches the event against its own linkage (tenantId for the tenant rail, providerSubscriptionId for the customer rail) and returns quietly when it is not its own. Declared for the same reason as payment:plan_usage and payment:plan_cache — payment processes charges and owns no subscriptions, and both rails require payment, so the arrow can only point inward. Before it, payment's webhook handler imported tenant_subscription directly and reacted on its behalf, which meant payment_subscription received NO gateway subscription events at all. Failure mode is neither sibling's: every rail runs (one rail's outage must not stop the other), then failures re-throw together so the provider retries and the log names the rail. Contributions must therefore be idempotent.

Asked when a stage is deleted (tasks.44): the module that OWNS a pipeline subject (its row carries its own stageId) moves its rows off the deleted stage, in the delete's transaction. Default export: (tenantId, { pipelineId, fromStageId, toStage: { stageId, isWon, isLost } | null }, manager) => Promise<{ subjectType, held, moved } | null>. With toStage null (no reassignment) it only counts its rows on the stage (`held`) and writes nothing; a non-zero count refuses the delete (409). With a target it moves every row on the stage there and applies its own won/lost bookkeeping. Fails closed: a contributor that throws or times out refuses the delete. Declared so pipeline never imports its subjects (tasks, crm_opportunity): the ledger alone used to be migrated, leaving the subject rows on a deleted stage.

Signs XML with a tenant's seal for a sandboxed plugin (broker capability crypto.signXml). Default export: an object with signXml(tenantId, xml, { keyKey, certKey, xpath?, prefix? }) returning { xml, signed }. The first contribution enabled for the tenant is used; with none (the e_signature module absent or switched off), the XML is returned unsigned, as when no seal is configured. A point rather than an import so that the plugin runtime (Core) never imports e_signature (Pro): docs/adr/0008.

Supplies the BASE unit price (minor units) for catalog products/variants, which pricing's rules then compute on. Default export: (tenantId, items: Array<{ productId, variantId? }>) => Promise<Map<string, MoneyMinor>> keyed 'productId' or 'productId:variantId'. OMIT an item you know nothing about — an absent key means PERCENT/FORMULA rules are SKIPPED for that item rather than computed against zero. Declared so pricing never imports commerce_catalog: a tenant with no catalog still prices manually-described quote lines. commerce_catalog contributes from store_products.basePrice.

Platform-level data a satellite holds about a user ACCOUNT — rows that exist once per account, not once per workspace (passkeys, personal API credentials, …). Default export: { erase({ userId }) => Promise<{ erased: number }> }. Runs during a self-service account deletion after the per-workspace `privacy:erasure` pass, sequentially, and a provider that throws is logged and skipped — the rest of the account is still erased. Distinct from `privacy:erasure`, which is called once per tenant with a tenantId; calling that per tenant for account-level rows would erase them on the first call and report zero thereafter.

Which subject populations a caller may act on, and whether they may execute destructive operations. Default export: { resolve(tenantId, { userId, tenantRole }) => Promise<{ subjectTypes?, canExecute? } | null> }. Contributions NARROW rather than widen — the base permission grants the right and a reader confines it, so a DPO scoped to customers never reaches employee subjects. Any reader may veto execution; none may grant it. Zero contributors is the intended default: with no reader the caller's permissions decide and every subject type is in scope. Those permissions are NOT all OWNER-level: privacy.requests.read / create / update / verify default to ADMIN (only privacy.dossier.build, privacy.requests.execute and privacy.policies.manage are OWNER), so without a reader every ADMIN reads every population's requests. Readers' subjectTypes are UNIONED: one reader returning ['*'] cancels another's confinement. A future scoping owner should therefore be a policy module, and the contract needs intersection / deny semantics before a second reader is added.

What a module holds about one data subject. Default export: { subjectTypes?, collect(tenantId, subject, { redactPii }) => Promise<DossierSection[]> }. MUST reuse the module's existing `tenant_export:collection` row producer, filtered by subject — the master plan (§66) is explicit that a contributor writes ONE producer and exposes it twice, because two independent collectors is the divergence shape the 2026-08 audit found repeatedly. Providers run concurrently. A provider that throws does not fail the dossier; the gap is recorded as a FAILED privacy_request_action and written into the artefact, because a compliance answer that silently omits a module is worse than one that names what it could not read.

Delete or anonymise what a module holds about a subject. Default export: { subjectTypes?, erase(tenantId, subject, { dryRun }) => Promise<{ erased, retained?, retainedReason?, mode? }> }. `dryRun` MUST be honoured — the operator flow previews before executing, and a provider that ignores the flag turns a preview into a deletion. The return type is not void on purpose: erasure is not absolute, and a module that must keep rows (statutory bookkeeping, open dispute, legal hold) reports them as `retained` with a reason, ideally citing a privacy_retention_policies row. A provider that erases NOTHING and keeps everything reports `mode: 'RETAIN'` — a named retention is an answer, silence is not, and an operator must be able to tell 'nothing held here' from 'held and kept on purpose'. Providers run SEQUENTIALLY because they write. The four existing hand-written eraseForUser implementations (commerce_review, commerce_wishlist, loyalty, user_social_account) are wrapped by contributions, not rewritten.

A Web Push delivery backend for browser subscriptions (VAPID). Sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @webpush/push) contribute their send op here; the payload encryption and the VAPID key stay host-side via the webpush capability. Native-app (Expo) subscriptions do not use this point: notification_push sends them to Expo in-tree (notification_push.expo.ts).

The session-ending orders a change that ends access must carry in its own transaction (D249): the host (user_session revoking sessions, tenant_member ending or changing a membership, tenant suspending, deleting or purging a tenant) calls recordSessionEndInTx(qr, cause) before its commit, and each contribution answers the orders the cause needs (ordersFor(cause) => SessionEndOrderInput[]; pure: no database, no Redis, never the host's transaction; every order names the cause's tenant). session_end records them in the host's transaction and delivers them after the commit. A contribution that fails or answers something invalid never blocks the change: it is logged, counted and left to its after-commit hook. Gate data, as the hosts' own hooks.

A kind of custom menu link a module offers (the dashboard's 'board'): the sysadmin picks a target of that kind in Platform -> Menu and, at each admin page load, the contributor turns it into a tenant-relative /admin path the viewer may open in their tenant, or into nothing. Default export: LinkTargetProvider { kind, label, suggest(q), validate(target), resolve(viewer, targets) }; kind must not be 'page' or 'url'. The resolved page's guard still applies. A contributor that fails hides only its own links. shell_menu imports nothing of the contributing module.
An SMS sending backend. Backends come from sandboxed marketplace plugins (e.g. @twilio/sms, @netgsm/sms); no in-tree module provides one, and the host reads plugins only.

A storage backend, chosen by the `storageProvider` setting. Backends come from sandboxed plugins only (e.g. @aws/s3, @minio/storage, and @local/storage for the key `local`: a directory on the server's own disk through the broker's `localfs` capability, for on-premise installs and for bootstrapping the plugin store); no in-tree module provides one, and the host reads plugins only.

A module adds a tab to a support ticket's page, in the agent's view and the requester's. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'support.ticket.tabs': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'support.ticket.tabs', component, order, props: { slotTabId, slotTabLabel } }; the page labels the tab 'support.detail.tab.<slotTabId>' with slotTabLabel as the English source. Props received: { tenantId, ticket, view: 'agent' | 'requester' }. Contributing makes neither module the other's dependency (EXT-14): without the contributor there is no tab.

A module declares an entity kind whose readings the store keeps (telemetry.kinds.ts `TelemetryEntityKind`): the kind name (`iot_device`, `fx.currency`), its keys (declared, or open with its own key rule and cap), its retention (a fixed class, or a resolver for plan-driven classes), `canRead(ctx, entityIds)` (record-level read check, default deny), whether dashboards may list it, whether a flow or a binding may write it (`acceptsExternalWrites`, narrowed by `canWrite`), its lane (table family) and its per-tenant write budget. Default export is the kind. The writer refuses an unregistered kind; every read path asks the kind's canRead. The registry of kinds is loaded on first use through the generated loaders (lazyContributors), so any module may contribute a kind without a contribution-chain cycle (analytics does, while automation contributes to analytics and telemetry to automation).

Fired once a call reaches a terminal state, with direction, timings, status and the resolved party. INVERTED rather than telephony importing `activity`: the registry scans dynamic `import()` too, so a lazy optional import is not available in this repo, and a hard `requires: ['activity']` would force a CRM activity log on every telephony tenant. This way `activity` is the contributor, a disabled `activity` simply yields zero contributions, and `activity` — which the 2026-08 audit records as having ZERO consumers — gets its first real one. Best-effort: a failing hook is logged, never fatal. Contributors write nothing when `party` is null; an activity attached to nothing is noise and the call is already durable here.

An extra step type for the inbound answering flow, e.g. `ai_agent` or `queue`. The core ships announcement, single-level digit menu, ring-agents, dial-external and voicemail; anything richer is contributed. Keeps the AI voice assistant out of the core (the model call belongs to `ai`, the media to the carrier) and reserves the seam `telephony_center` will use for queues without the core learning what a queue is. An unknown verb is a flow error, but the engine always falls through to a safe terminal step — a caller must never meet silence because an operator mis-edited a menu.

Reverse phone lookup: `(tenantId, e164, {limit, signal}) => Promise<PartyMatch[]>`, where PartyMatch carries a contributor-owned `partyType` tag ('CONTACT', 'LEAD', 'TICKET'), a display label and an optional owning user. INVERTED on purpose, the `calendar:busy_source` / `commerce_catalog:stock_source` direction: telephony RESOLVES and domains CONTRIBUTE, so this module requires neither `contact` nor `crm_lead` and a CRM-less tenant can still run a call centre. FAIL-OPEN with a hard 300ms budget: a contributor that throws or is slow is dropped and the call rings with a bare number — a broken CRM must never stop a phone from being answered. Deliberately the opposite of the carrier adapters, which fail closed (telephony.provider.types.ts), and the two reasons are written down together so the asymmetry reads as a decision.

Who owns the outcome of an AUTOMATED call (telephony.scripted.service.ts): the module that asked for a call that speaks a script and gathers one key press, e.g. on_call paging a person. Default export: { onDigits(tenantId, { token, digits }) => Promise<{ outcome: 'accepted' | 'ignored' | 'refused' }> }, selected by the key the requester put in the call's signed token. Telephony verifies the carrier's signature and its own token, then hands over the digits and the requester's OWN single-use credential for this call; what a key means (on-call: 1 acknowledges the page) is the handler's business and telephony never learns what a page is. INVERTED so telephony imports no requester. A handler that is missing or throws answers 'refused': the call says the page can no longer be acknowledged and hangs up. The requester reaches telephony through `TelephonyScriptedCallService` (an optional `import()` on its side); this module imports no requester and contributes nothing back to one.

The zone domains this deployment's tenants' base domains must sit inside (docs/phases/02-fleet/14-zones-and-central-signup.md, F43): an address under a zone must mean data in that zone's region. Default export: () => Promise<{ zones: string[] } | null> (null = no restriction). Asked only on a fleet node; no contribution = no restriction. A contribution that throws, times out or is paused refuses new base domains (fail closed); existing ones keep serving. Exists so tenant_domain never imports the fleet: fleet_agent answers it from the installed trust bundle.

A module contributes its OWN tenant-scoped data to the tenant export. Default export: (tenantId, { redactPii }) => Promise<{ key, label, rows }[]>. tenant_export resolves; the owning module contributes — it cannot import 90 modules to export them. Additive: the built-in collections in tenant_export.collect.ts are unchanged and a contribution may NOT claim one of their keys (refused and reported, never allowed to shadow). Namespace your key with the module (invoiceLines, supportTickets); the export document is flat. A contributor that throws does not fail the export, but the gap is written into the artifact as `collectionErrors` — a compliance export that silently omits a module looks complete, which is worse than one that names what it could not read. redactPii is applied by tenant_export AFTER the merge, so a contributor cannot opt its rows out of it.

Told after an ACTIVE member's built-in role or custom roles changed, with { tenantId, userId, reason: 'role' | 'role_keys', sessionEndOrderedBy? } (D249, as membership_ended). Default export: (changed) => Promise<void>. For things granted once and kept that must follow the new rights: websocket_session drops the member's sockets in the workspace so they come back with tickets minted under the new role (websocket.08). Ending a membership is tenant_member:membership_ended. Best-effort by contract: a hook that throws is logged and skipped.

A header button of the Members page (/admin/members) that opens another module's panel in a right-side drawer, as the Devices page opens "Awaiting approval (n)": "Invitations (n)" (tenant_invitation, the pending invitations). The sidebar has no item for it (docs/phases/45-install-config, owner 2026-10-27). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'tenant_member.members.drawers': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'tenant_member.members.drawers', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { drawerId, label, labelKey } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, open, onCount, onClose } (common/ui/slot-drawers.component). It stays mounted while its drawer is shut, draws its panel only while open, and may report the number its button shows through onCount. The page shows a button only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions, isolates each in an error boundary, and opens the drawer whose drawerId is in `?tab=` on arrival (the old tab's link, /admin/members?tab=invitations). tenant_member imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

Told after a member stops being an ACTIVE member of a workspace (removed, suspended, deprovisioned), with { tenantId, userId, reason, sessionEndOrderedBy? } (D249: the modules whose session_end:order_source orders the membership's own transaction already recorded; their hooks skip it). Default export: (ended) => Promise<void>. For things addressed to the person because they were a member and that must stop the moment they are not — notification_push deletes their push registrations for the workspace, otherwise a removed member's phone keeps receiving the workspace's notifications. Best-effort by contract: a hook that throws is logged and skipped, removing someone must never fail because a satellite's cleanup had trouble.

A ready-made custom group a tenant can add in one click (Access control > Groups > From template). Default export: { key (lowercase role key), label, description?, permissions: string[] }. Contributions with the SAME key merge, and each module lists only its OWN permissions (e.g. commerce_order + commerce_fulfillment + commerce_return + commerce_review make store_operator). Offered permissions are filtered to the tenant's enabled modules, and a template left empty is not offered. Exists because lowering a permission's minRole to USER also grants it to every storefront shopper (sign-up makes them USER members); a group grants it only to the staff it is assigned to.

A ceiling on the number of members beyond the plan's `max_members` limit: the seats a tenant's entitlements include, with the admin override. Default export: { effectiveLimit(tenantId) => Promise<number | null> } implementing SeatAllowanceProvider; null states no ceiling. Consulted when a member is added, where the tightest ceiling of all contributors applies. Declared so `tenant_member`, the tenancy primitive, never imports the module that sells seats.

A holder of seats that are spoken for but not yet ACTIVE members. Default export: { countReserved(tenantId) } implementing SeatReservationProvider. Consulted at ISSUE time — when a tenant adds a member or sends an invitation — so the plan's `max_members` ceiling counts unclaimed seats too; without it a tenant could issue unlimited invitations under the cap and let every acceptance walk in unchecked. A contributor that throws is treated as zero rather than refusing the operation: an unrelated module's outage must not look like a billing refusal. Declared so `tenant_member`, the primitive invitations are built on, never imports them back.

failOpen.reason: A quota guard: an unavailable reservation source undercounts reserved seats, so an invite may pass a plan limit; refusing every invite because a contributor broke is the worse failure (EXT-3).

extensionPoints.description: Who reviews a setting change while the tenant's maker-checker is on (`tenantSettingMakerChecker`). Default export: SettingChangeReviewer { submit(tenantId, { key, value, encrypted, actorId }) => Promise<{ reviewId }> }; the value is stored encrypted for a secret key. The approval module contributes it (the shared approval queue) and, on a terminal decision, calls tenant_setting's applySettingChangeDecision from its own approval-phase boot task. The first active reviewer is used. Fails closed: with maker-checker on and no active reviewer (approval missing or off for the tenant) the write is refused with 409 before anything is saved, because maker-checker is a security control. Declared here so tenant_setting never imports approval, which requires it.

An extra entry on the settings overview (/admin/settings), in the Access & Security grid. Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'tenant_setting.settings.links': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'tenant_setting.settings.links', component, order, scope: 'tenant' }. Props received: { tenantId }. The contribution renders its own link card and decides itself whether it applies (it may render nothing, e.g. the fleet node's residency facts off a node). Declared so tenant_setting never imports the satellite that owns the page.

A module declares the catalogue bundle it is sold in, without editing tenant_subscription.catalog-data.ts: the contribution key is the bundle key (bundle_<name>) and puts ONLY the contributing module in that bundle. Static metadata (validated by ContributedBundleSchema, tenant_subscription.catalog-bundles.ts): { name? (required for a new key), workspace?, visibility?: 'public' | 'private', features?: { <feature key>: <LIMIT number, -1 = unlimited> | true (BOOLEAN) }, featureOnly?: boolean, billing?: 'once', price?: { retail, wholesale } (default USD, monthly or one-time) }. Several modules joining one key form one bundle; a shipped bundle keeps its own name, workspace, visibility, price and billing, and a contribution may join it. `features` are what the bundle grants while a tenant holds it as an add-on (LIMITs merge to the larger, BOOLEANs with OR): the seed and the sync write them onto the bundle product and the gate reads them (resolvePlanFeatures), so an add-on sold beside any plan (the IoT package, ADR-0013) carries its own quotas. `featureOnly: true` sells features of the contributing module, not the module (docs/phases/07-dashboard/31 C7, the SCADA pieces): the module goes to the product's `requiresModules`, never its `moduleIds`, and the store offers the product only to tenants entitled to every required module; a feature-only and a module contribution never share a key. `billing: 'once'` makes a contributed bundle a one-time purchase only (E6). A contribution may not grant a piece key another module declares through feature_gate:pieces (ADR-0015, a module sells only its own pieces): such a contribution is refused whole. Read by seedBundleCatalog, syncBundleCatalog, the full-load seed and the catalogue coverage test; metadata only, no code is loaded.

Legacy grants (docs/phases/07-dashboard/31 E5): a module that starts selling something it used to give away answers, for one tenant, which catalogue products the tenant should be comped for because it already built with them. Default export: LegacyGrantProvider { legacyGrants(tenantId, { asOf }) => Promise<Array<{ product: <product key>, reason: string }>> }, reading only that tenant's own data as it stood at asOf, the contribution's cut-over (recorded once per deployment by the first run with monetization on that finds one of its products ACTIVE; anything created or changed after it does not count); throw when the answer cannot be read completely. Metadata: `products`, every product key the contribution may ask for (an answer naming another one is ignored), and `label`. tenant_subscription's hourly sweep (and one run at boot) asks each contribution ONCE per tenant and records it (`tenant_legacy_grant_runs`); it grants each product as a permanent operator comp (source admin_grant, no end date, audited, the reason on the row) through the comp path, only a product the contributing module itself contributes to tenant_subscription:bundle (another module's product, or one an operator made, is skipped as not_own, ADR-0015), and of those only an ACTIVE platform bundle or add-on that grants nothing beyond the contributing module (the module itself, or its own pieces declared through feature_gate:pieces, through requiresModules; any other feature, another module's piece or a platform LIMIT or BOOLEAN among them, refuses it as not_grantable). A product the tenant already holds for good is skipped, an archived one too; a product the catalogue does not hold yet, or holds inactive, keeps the tenant pending for a later run, and so does a failing or timed-out contribution. Nothing runs while monetization is off. Behaviour gate: a contributor that is off for the tenant is asked once it is on.

A header button of the Plan & Billing page (/admin/subscription) that opens another module's panel in a right-side drawer, as the Devices page opens "Awaiting approval (n)": "Usage" (tenant_usage). The sidebar has no item for it (docs/phases/45-install-config, owner 2026-10-27). Implemented through the CLIENT slot 'tenant_subscription.subscription.drawers': a contributor declares slots[] = { slot: 'tenant_subscription.subscription.drawers', component, order, scope: 'tenant', permissions, props: { drawerId, label, labelKey } }; the component default-exports a function of { tenantId, open, onCount, onClose } (common/ui/slot-drawers.component). It stays mounted while its drawer is shut, draws its panel only while open, and may report the number its button shows through onCount. The page shows a button only when its module is on and the viewer holds its permissions, isolates each in an error boundary, and opens the drawer whose drawerId is in `?tab=` on arrival (the old tab's link, /admin/subscription?tab=usage). tenant_subscription imports none of the contributors (EXT-14).

A module declares a period metric it increments through TenantUsageService.increment/incrementBatch, without editing tenant_usage. The declaration is the contribution's static metadata: { label, unit, period: 'month' | 'day', quotaKey? } with the contribution key as the metric key (lowerCamel, stable forever); quotaKey names the feature_gate LIMIT it is enforced against (feature_gate.period-quota / tenant_usage.quota).
